E.tempting: evaluates for upper airway obstruction

F.fit: Not here: not routinely recommended in infant bronchiolitis, hypoxemia takes priority

G.fit: Here: 4-month-old, intercostal retractions, wheezes, oxygen saturation 84%

H.fit: Not here: systemic epinephrine is contraindicated for routine infant bronchiolitis
H.tempting: potent bronchodilator used in severe pediatric airway distress

nodes.text: Hypoxemia (saturation 84%) + respiratory distress: immediate airway assessment + continuous pulse oximetry
Administration of humidified supplemental oxygen via nasal cannula to maintain saturation >= 90%
Nasal suctioning with saline drops to clear upper airway secretions before feeds
Assess hydration: initiate IV fluids or nasogastric feeds if tachypneic infant cannot feed safely
Routine bronchodilators, systemic corticosteroids, and antibiotics are not recommended
**Escalating work of breathing or persistent hypoxemia:** trial heated humidified high-flow nasal cannula
**Impending respiratory failure or severe apnea:** endotracheal intubation and mechanical ventilation

c-peds-03-q047.boardCall: Infant apnea + bilateral retinal hemorrhages + subdural hemorrhage -> acceleration-deceleration head injury (abusive head trauma)
c-peds-03-q047.hinge: Repetitive acceleration-deceleration shearing forces (shaken baby syndrome) cause tearing of bridging veins and multilayered retinal hemorrhages.
c-peds-03-q047.trap: Simple blunt trauma or accidental falls in an infant do not produce extensive bilateral multilayered retinal hemorrhages or interhemispheric subdural hematoma.

A.clue: Rotational shearing forces tearing bridging veins
A.fit: Here: unresponsive infant, bilateral retinal hemorrhages, acute subdural hemorrhage

B.fit: Not here: devastating acute brain injury with subdural bleeding and edema
B.tempting: infant suddenly cried, became limp, and stopped breathing

C.fit: Not here: extensive intracranial hemorrhage, edema, and retinal hemorrhages
C.tempting: explains sudden apnea and cyanosis around bath time

D.clue: Direct focal impact without rotational shear
D.fit: Not here: lacks diffuse rotational shear causing interhemispheric subdural and retinal hemorrhages
D.tempting: common mechanical etiology of traumatic brain injury

E.clue: Submersion asphyxia and hypoxic brain injury
E.fit: Not here: occurred before entering bath, acute subdural and retinal hemorrhages
E.tempting: event occurred in bathroom prior to bath

F.fit: Not here: does not cause rotational subdural hemorrhage or retinal hemorrhages
F.tempting: causes acute pediatric apnea and cyanosis

nodes.text: Unresponsive infant + retinal hemorrhages + subdural hematoma: secure airway + emergent neuroresuscitation
Rotational acceleration-deceleration forces tear bridging veins causing subdural hemorrhage and diffuse axonal injury
Emergent noncontrast head CT + neurosurgical consultation to evaluate for surgical hematoma evacuation
Targeted intracranial pressure (ICP) management: hypertonic saline + head elevation + avoid hyperventilation
Complete skeletal survey + dilated ophthalmology examination to document occult fractures and retinal hemorrhages
Immediate notification of Child Protective Services (CPS) + social work + hospital child protection team

c-peds-03-q048.boardCall: 2-month-old + grade 3/6 holosystolic murmur with thrill at lower left sternal border + left atrial enlargement -> ventricular septal defect
c-peds-03-q048.hinge: A harsh holosystolic murmur and systolic thrill loudest at the lower left sternal border with left atrial volume overload define a ventricular septal defect.
c-peds-03-q048.trap: Atrial septal defect causes a systolic ejection murmur at the upper left border with fixed split S2, not a harsh holosystolic murmur with thrill.

A.clue: Systolic ejection murmur at right upper sternal border
A.fit: Not here: holosystolic murmur at lower left sternal border with thrill
A.tempting: causes systolic murmur and precordial thrill

B.clue: Midsystolic murmur at LUSB with fixed split S2
B.fit: Not here: harsh holosystolic murmur with palpable systolic thrill
B.tempting: causes pediatric left-to-right cardiac shunting

C.clue: Systolic ejection murmur with early click
C.fit: Not here: pansystolic murmur at lower left border, enlarged left atrium
C.tempting: causes prominent systolic murmur and thrill

D.clue: Cyanotic anomaly with single S2 and ejection murmur
D.fit: Not here: acyanotic infant with normal oxygenation and holosystolic murmur
D.tempting: includes a large ventricular septal defect

E.fit: Here: grade 3/6 holosystolic murmur, thrill at LLSB, enlarged left atrium

nodes.text: Holosystolic murmur + thrill at lower left sternal border: transthoracic echocardiography is diagnostic test of choice
Echocardiography defines VSD size, anatomic location, and hemodynamic shunt ratio
Small muscular or perimembranous VSD: clinical observation with reassurance, as most close spontaneously
**Large VSD with failure to thrive or heart failure:** initiate oral furosemide + ACE inhibitor
Optimize caloric intake with high-calorie infant formula to support optimal infant growth
**Persistent heart failure or pulmonary hypertension:** surgical patch closure within first 6-12 months

Femoral pulses are equal

c-peds-03-q049.boardCall: Paroxysmal coughing spells + cyanosis + posttussive vomiting in 2-month-old -> pertussis (Bordetella pertussis)
c-peds-03-q049.hinge: Violent coughing paroxysms accompanied by facial cyanosis and posttussive emesis in an unvaccinated 2-month-old indicate pertussis.
c-peds-03-q049.trap: Chlamydial pneumonia in young infants causes a staccato cough, but presents with tachypnea, crackles, and lack of violent paroxysms or cyanotic pauses.

A.fit: Not here: prolonged 20-second coughing paroxysms with cyanotic episodes
A.tempting: cough followed by vomiting suggests gastroesophageal reflux

B.clue: Staccato paroxysmal cough with lung crackles
B.fit: Not here: clear lungs without crackles, violent paroxysms with cyanosis
B.tempting: causes paroxysmal coughing spells in 2-month-old infant

C.fit: Not here: appears healthy between coughing spells, clear lung exam
C.tempting: causes cyanosis and respiratory symptoms in infant

D.fit: Here: 20-second coughing spells, cyanosis for 10 seconds, posttussive vomiting

E.clue: Distal airway obstruction with wheezing and fever
E.fit: Not here: no crackles or wheezes on chest auscultation, posttussive vomiting
E.tempting: common viral respiratory cause of infant cough and apnea

nodes.text: Paroxysmal coughing + posttussive emesis or apnea in infant: immediately admit to hospital for monitoring
Droplet isolation precautions + obtain nasopharyngeal swab for Bordetella pertussis PCR and culture
Start oral azithromycin for 5 days immediately without waiting for laboratory confirmation
Complete blood count: marked absolute lymphocytosis supports clinical diagnosis
**Hyperleukocytosis (> 50,000/mm3) or refractory hypoxemia:** intensive care for exchange transfusion
Prescribe prophylactic azithromycin to all household contacts regardless of immunization status

frequently followed by vomiting
Coughing continues for 20 seconds, at which time he appears cyanotic
No crackles are heard on auscultation of the chest
2-month-old boy is brought to the physician

c-peds-03-q050.hinge: Bilious vomiting and bowel ischemia (bloody stool, peritonitis) in the first week of life result from midgut volvulus due to failed 270-degree bowel rotation.
c-peds-03-q050.trap: Duodenal atresia results from failed recanalization, but causes non-ischemic obstruction on day 1 with double bubble rather than volvulus shock on day 7.

A.clue: Viscous inspissated secretions causing meconium ileus
A.fit: Not here: acute presentation on day 7 with bilious emesis and volvulus shock
A.tempting: causes neonatal bowel obstruction and feeding intolerance

B.clue: Failed recanalization of embryonic gut lumen
B.fit: Not here: double-bubble present at birth, lacks volvulus ischemia and bloody stool
B.tempting: causes neonatal bilious vomiting

C.clue: Absent myenteric and submucosal plexus ganglion cells
C.fit: Not here: acute midgut volvulus with bilious vomiting and bowel necrosis
C.tempting: causes pediatric intestinal obstruction and enterocolitis

D.fit: Here: 7-day-old, bilious vomiting, bloody stool, hypotension, peritonitis

E.fit: Not here: presents immediately at birth with distention and triple-bubble pattern
E.tempting: causes congenital intestinal obstruction and ischemic bowel

nodes.text: Bilious vomiting + shock (BP 65/35) + peritonitis: immediate NPO + NG tube decompression + rapid IV fluid resuscitation
Failure of normal counterclockwise 270-degree bowel rotation leads to narrow mesenteric base
Midgut twists around superior mesenteric vessels causing acute intestinal strangulation and bloody stools
Upper GI series: corkscrew duodenum or ligament of Treitz to the right of midline
Empiric broad-spectrum IV antibiotics (ampicillin, gentamicin, metronidazole) for enteric translocation
**Peritonitis or shock present:** emergent exploratory laparotomy with Ladd procedure
**Frankly necrotic bowel segments:** bowel resection with temporary enterostomy

acute-otitis-media.name: Acute otitis media
acute-otitis-media.scope: Bulging erythematous tympanic membrane, impaired mobility, oral amoxicillin first-line, amoxicillin-clavulanate, tympanostomy indications
acute-otitis-media.core: Acute otalgia with middle-ear effusion and a bulging tympanic membrane identifies acute otitis media; age, laterality, and severity guide antibiotics.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Young age, daycare, viral URI, tobacco smoke exposure, absent breastfeeding
Craniofacial abnormalities and eustachian tube dysfunction increase recurrence

rows.label: Clues
items: Ear tugging, fever, irritability, poor feeding; spontaneous perforation causes new otorrhea
★ **Postauricular swelling/tenderness, protruding pinna** → mastoiditis
Erythematous membrane alone, especially during crying, insufficient for diagnosis

rows.label: Pathophys
items: URI-related eustachian edema traps fluid; pneumococcus, nontypeable H influenzae, Moraxella commonly infect middle ear

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **Pneumatic otoscopy**: reduced mobility supports effusion; moderate/severe bulging or nonexternal otorrhea diagnostic
Mild bulging requires recent otalgia or intense erythema; no effusion → no AOM diagnosis
Tympanometry if effusion uncertain; routine imaging and cultures unnecessary
Failure after 48–72 h → repeat examination; persistent effusion alone does not mean antibiotic failure

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ **Acetaminophen or ibuprofen** for pain regardless of antibiotic decision
★ When treating → **amoxicillin 80–90 mg/kg/day**; 10 days if <2 years or severe
Recent amoxicillin within 30 days, purulent conjunctivitis, or amoxicillin failure → amoxicillin-clavulanate
Selected older nonsevere cases → 5–7 days; severe illness/complication or oral intolerance changes regimen
★ Recurrent AOM **≥3/6 months or ≥4/12 months** → tube evaluation; effusion required at candidacy assessment

rows.label: Complications
items: Conductive hearing loss, membrane perforation, mastoiditis, rare intracranial infection
Effusion ≥3 months → hearing assessment; tubes considered for bilateral persistent fluid with hearing difficulty

rows.label: Prevention
items: Pneumococcal/influenza vaccination, breastfeeding, smoke avoidance; no routine prophylactic antibiotics
Observe speech/hearing development in recurrent disease

rows.label: Mimics
items: Otitis media with effusion: fluid without acute inflammatory illness
Otitis externa: canal inflammation, pain with tragus/pinna movement
Referred dental/TMJ pain: normal middle-ear examination

angioedema.name: Angioedema
angioedema.scope: Hereditary angioedema (C1 esterase inhibitor deficiency, C4 level), ACE inhibitor-induced, mast cell-mediated vs bradykinin-mediated, acute airway compromise, C1-INH concentrate, icatibant
angioedema.core: Deep, transient swelling of lips, tongue, airway, or bowel; distinguishing histamine from bradykinin determines which drugs will work.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Allergens, NSAIDs, insect stings → mast cell activation
Hereditary attacks: autosomal dominant history, trauma, dental procedures, estrogen exposure
ACE inhibitors: attacks possible even after years of uneventful use

rows.label: Clues
items: Nonpitting, asymmetric edema; gastrointestinal attacks may cause severe colicky pain, vomiting
★ Hoarseness, stridor, drooling, rapidly progressive tongue swelling → **airway emergency**
Recurrent episodes beginning in childhood support hereditary disease; late onset suggests acquired deficiency

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Histamine increases vascular permeability through mast cell mediator release
C1-INH deficiency/dysfunction or impaired bradykinin breakdown → kallikrein-mediated vascular leakage

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ Recurrent nonurticarial attacks → **C4 plus C1-INH level and function**; repeat abnormal results
Low C1-INH quantity → type I; normal/high quantity with low function → type II
Normal C4 does not fully exclude HAE; C1q low in acquired, usually normal in hereditary disease
ACE inhibitor-related disease: clinical diagnosis; complement usually normal

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Secure threatened airway early with expert intubation; prepare surgical airway
Uncertain mechanism with possible anaphylaxis → IM epinephrine immediately; do not await complement testing
★ ACE inhibitor-related: stop drug permanently; airway/supportive care; targeted drug evidence inconsistent
HAE attack: give available on-demand drug early; plasma if specific agents unavailable

rows.label: Complications
items: Asphyxiation, hypovolemia from bowel edema; unnecessary abdominal surgery after misdiagnosis
Recurrence may continue after ACE inhibitor discontinuation

rows.label: Prevention
items: ★ HAE: on-demand rescue supply; procedure prophylaxis with C1-INH; avoid ACE inhibitors and estrogen
Frequent HAE attacks → lanadelumab, berotralstat, or scheduled C1-INH; screen first-degree relatives

rows.label: Mimics
items: Cellulitis: persistent warm, tender erythema with infection signs
Contact dermatitis: superficial pruritic, eczematous eruption rather than isolated deep swelling

table.title: Mediator guides treatment
rows: Epinephrine for anaphylaxis; H1 antihistamine adjunct

bronchiectasis.name: Bronchiectasis
bronchiectasis.scope: Cystic fibrosis, post-infectious, high-resolution CT, airway clearance, pseudomonas colonization, acute exacerbation
bronchiectasis.core: Chronic productive cough with recurrent respiratory infections and permanently dilated bronchi on high-resolution CT.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Cystic fibrosis, prior severe pneumonia/TB, primary ciliary dyskinesia, aspiration, immunodeficiency
ABPA, rheumatoid arthritis, obstructing endobronchial lesion; some cases remain idiopathic

rows.label: Clues
items: Copious purulent sputum, coarse crackles, recurrent focal infections, hemoptysis, sometimes clubbing
Exacerbation: increased sputum volume/purulence, cough, dyspnea, fatigue; hypoxemia or sepsis → severe disease
Early lifelong infections, sinusitis, infertility, or situs inversus suggest impaired ciliary clearance

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Impaired mucus clearance → persistent infection and neutrophilic inflammation → irreversible airway wall destruction

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **High-resolution chest CT**: signet-ring bronchi, absent tapering, airways visible near pleura
Sputum bacterial and mycobacterial cultures; spirometry measures associated airflow limitation
Quantitative immunoglobulins; total IgE/Aspergillus testing for ABPA; sweat chloride if CF suspected
Localized disease → bronchoscopy for tumor/foreign body; diffuse disease → investigate systemic cause

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Daily **airway clearance**, exercise; bronchodilator for obstruction; no routine inhaled steroids or non-CF dornase alfa
★ Exacerbation → sputum culture then antibiotics guided by prior isolates; often **14 days**
Pseudomonas susceptible → ciprofloxacin; severe infection → IV cefepime or piperacillin-tazobactam
★ ≥2 yearly or ≥1 severe exacerbation → azithromycin after NTM exclusion; chronic Pseudomonas → inhaled tobramycin
Massive hemoptysis → airway protection and bronchial artery embolization; focal refractory disease → resection evaluation

rows.label: Complications
items: Chronic Pseudomonas colonization, resistant infection, respiratory failure, pulmonary hypertension
Antibiotic toxicity/resistance; macrolides can cause QT prolongation and hearing impairment

rows.label: Prevention
items: Smoking cessation, influenza/pneumococcal vaccination, aspiration management, treatment of underlying immunodeficiency
New Pseudomonas isolation → specialist eradication regimen, often ciprofloxacin followed by inhaled antibiotic

rows.label: Mimics
items: Chronic bronchitis: smoking-related sputum without characteristic bronchial dilation
Lung abscess: focal cavitary lesion with air-fluid level
Pulmonary TB: constitutional illness and compatible imaging; mycobacterial testing confirms

bronchiolitis.name: Bronchiolitis
bronchiolitis.scope: Respiratory syncytial virus (RSV), infant wheezing, respiratory distress, hypoxemia, supplemental oxygen, nasal suctioning, palivizumab prophylaxis indications
bronchiolitis.core: Infant with a viral prodrome followed by a first episode of diffuse wheezing or crackles: supportive care is the main treatment.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Age <2 years, winter exposure, daycare; RSV commonest cause
Severe disease: age <12 weeks, prematurity, chronic lung disease, significant congenital heart disease, immunodeficiency

rows.label: Clues
items: Tachypnea, retractions, nasal flaring, reduced intake; examination may fluctuate after suctioning
★ Apnea, exhaustion, cyanosis, dehydration → admission and escalation
Very young infants may present with apnea without prominent lower-airway findings

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Viral injury → small-airway edema, mucus plugging, air trapping, patchy atelectasis
Ventilation–perfusion mismatch causes hypoxemia; tiny infant airways increase obstruction

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **Clinical diagnosis**; no routine chest radiograph, viral testing, CBC, or blood cultures
Assess work of breathing, hydration, and oxygenation; investigate focal findings or atypical course
Radiographic atelectasis can mimic pneumonia and drive unnecessary antibiotics

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Gentle **nasal suctioning** + small frequent feeds; NG/IV fluids if intake inadequate
★ Persistent SpO2 <90% → oxygen; worsening distress → high-flow support, CPAP/intubation if failing
No routine albuterol, epinephrine, corticosteroids, antibiotics, or chest physiotherapy
Antibiotics only for documented/suspected bacterial coinfection; avoid deep repetitive suctioning

rows.label: Complications
items: Respiratory failure, apnea, dehydration; later recurrent wheezing association
Cough may persist for weeks despite improving respiratory effort

rows.label: Prevention
items: ★ Hand hygiene, smoke avoidance; maternal RSV vaccine or infant antibody protection
Age <8 months: nirsevimab/clesrovimab if maternal vaccination absent/unknown or birth <14 days afterward
Age 8–19 months, second season: nirsevimab for selected high-risk children, including severe immunocompromise
Palivizumab: historical board option; US availability ended 2025; current long-acting antibodies replace it

rows.label: Mimics
items: Asthma: recurrent episodes, older child, atopic history
Foreign body: abrupt onset, unilateral wheeze
Bacterial pneumonia: focal consolidation, toxic appearance

caustic-ingestion.name: Caustic ingestion
caustic-ingestion.scope: Acid and alkali ingestion, airway assessment, contraindications to emesis or neutralization, early esophagogastroduodenoscopy within 24 hours, stricture complications
caustic-ingestion.core: Corrosive ingestion can burn the airway and gastrointestinal tract; a normal mouth examination does not exclude deep injury.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Young children: accidental household cleaner exposure; adults: intentional large-volume ingestion
Drain cleaners, oven cleaners, industrial acids; concentration and contact duration determine severity

rows.label: Clues
items: Drooling, odynophagia, dysphagia, vomiting, hematemesis, chest or abdominal pain
★ **Stridor, hoarseness, respiratory distress** → threatened airway
Severe tenderness, rigidity, fever, shock → transmural necrosis or perforation

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Alkali: liquefactive necrosis, deep esophageal penetration; acid: coagulative necrosis, often gastric injury
Both agents can injure the entire upper gastrointestinal tract; eschar provides incomplete protection

rows.label: Dx
items: Identify substance, concentration, amount, time; poison control consultation
★ Stable symptomatic/significant exposure → **EGD within 24 hours** for injury grading
Suspected perforation/necrosis → contrast CT chest/abdomen and surgery consultation; avoid diagnostic endoscopy if perforated
CBC, electrolytes, renal function, lactate, blood gas; normal labs cannot exclude injury

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ **Airway first**; early controlled intubation with direct visualization when swelling progresses
NPO, IV crystalloid, analgesia; surgical treatment for perforation or full-thickness necrosis
★ **No emesis, neutralization, gastric lavage, or activated charcoal**; additional burns or heat generation
Avoid blind NG placement; no routine corticosteroids or prophylactic antibiotics

rows.label: Complications
items: Mediastinitis, peritonitis, hemorrhage, fistula; delayed esophageal stricture or gastric outlet obstruction
Long-term esophageal squamous cell carcinoma risk; strictures may require repeated dilation

rows.label: Prevention
items: Locked storage in original labeled containers; never transfer chemicals into beverage bottles
Intentional ingestion → psychiatric assessment after stabilization; swallowing/nutrition follow-up after severe injury

rows.label: Mimics
items: Esophageal foreign body: discrete obstruction on history or imaging
Pill esophagitis: medication exposure, focal ulceration without extensive chemical burns

caustic-ingestion.evidence: Not checked online; established toxicology teaching.

child-abuse-and-neglect.name: Child abuse and neglect
child-abuse-and-neglect.scope: Physical abuse (burn patterns, fractures of different ages, metaphyseal corner fractures), abusive head trauma (shaken baby, subdural hematoma, retinal hemorrhages), neglect, mandatory reporting
child-abuse-and-neglect.core: Reasonable suspicion of child maltreatment requires protective reporting; proof and caregiver permission are unnecessary.

rows.label: Principle
items: Inconsistent history, delayed care, or developmentally impossible mechanism increase suspicion

rows.label: Do
items: ★ **Report to child protective services** promptly; urgent danger → emergency protective services
Stabilize; document verbatim statements, findings and photographs; interview caregivers separately
★ Suspected physical abuse age <2 → **skeletal survey**; repeat after approximately 2 weeks

rows.label: Don't
items: Confront or accuse caregivers; promise secrecy; delay reporting for complete diagnostic certainty
Discharge into an unsafe setting; substitute reporting to a supervisor for mandated reporting

rows.label: Exceptions
items: Financial hardship alone ≠ neglect; assess ability to obtain food, shelter and medical care
Consider bleeding disorders, osteogenesis imperfecta and accidental trauma without delaying protection

rows.label: Traps
items: ★ **Metaphyseal corner/posterior rib fractures**; mixed healing stages → abuse concern
Immersion burns: uniform depth, sharp edges, stocking/glove pattern; nonmobile infants: sentinel bruising
★ Abusive head trauma: **subdural hemorrhage, extensive retinal hemorrhages**, unexplained encephalopathy

table.title: Presentation → evaluation
rows: AST/ALT, lipase, urinalysis; CT if concerning
Growth, nutrition, hygiene, supervision, unmet care needs

child-abuse-and-neglect.evidence: Not checked online; established pediatric safeguarding principles; reporting procedures vary by jurisdiction.

childhood-and-adolescent-immunizations.name: Childhood and adolescent immunizations
childhood-and-adolescent-immunizations.scope: Routine pediatric vaccine schedule, adolescent immunizations (meningococcal conjugate, HPV, Tdap), catch-up vaccination guidelines
childhood-and-adolescent-immunizations.core: Vaccinate before exposure; use age, prior doses, minimum intervals, and immune status to choose the next dose.

rows.label: Who
items: All children; AAP 2026 schedule retains broad routine childhood protection

rows.label: Schedule
items: ★ 11–12 years: **Tdap, MenACWY**; MenACWY booster at 16 years
AAP HPV: start 9–12 years; <15 years → two doses, 6–12 months apart
HPV initiation ≥15 years or immunocompromised → three doses at 0, 1–2, 6 months

rows.label: Special groups
items: ★ Catch-up: **never restart**; respect minimum ages and intervals
Asplenia/complement defects: extra meningococcal/pneumococcal doses; annual influenza from 6 months
HBsAg-positive mother: HepB vaccine + HBIG within 12 hours of birth

rows.label: Choice
items: MenB: shared decision, usually 16–23 years; high-risk patients need earlier protection

rows.label: Contraindications
items: ★ Live vaccines: pregnancy, severe immunodeficiency; prior anaphylaxis precludes that vaccine
Rotavirus: SCID or prior intussusception; first dose by 14 weeks 6 days

rows.label: Traps
items: ★ **AAP/classic boards: multidose HPV**; federal 2026 policy: one dose
Mild illness, antibiotics, breastfeeding → vaccination proceeds; rotavirus series ends by 8 months
Separate injectable live vaccines ≥4 weeks unless simultaneous; IVIG can delay MMR/varicella

table.title: Routine AAP childhood schedule
rows: First vaccination <9 years: two ≥4 weeks apart

chlamydia-infection.name: Chlamydia infection
chlamydia-infection.scope: Chlamydia trachomatis, nongonococcal urethritis, cervicitis, lymphogranuloma venereum, neonatal conjunctivitis and pneumonia, NAAT screening and diagnosis, doxycycline and azithromycin
chlamydia-infection.core: Often silent sexually transmitted intracellular infection causing urethritis or cervicitis; untreated infection threatens fertility and can infect newborns during delivery.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Age <25 years, new/multiple partners, inconsistent condom use, infected partner; perinatal exposure

rows.label: Clues
items: Dysuria, scant discharge, sterile pyuria; friable cervix, mucopurulent discharge, postcoital bleeding
★ Neonatal conjunctivitis at **5–12 days**; afebrile staccato pneumonia at **1–3 months**
LGV: transient painless genital ulcer → tender inguinal nodes/buboes or invasive proctocolitis

rows.label: Pathophys
items: C. trachomatis: obligate intracellular bacterium; D–K serovars cause genital/perinatal infection, L1–L3 cause LGV

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **NAAT**: vaginal swab preferred in women; first-catch urine in men; rectal swab after exposure
Test for gonorrhea, HIV, syphilis; fever/pelvic pain → evaluate for PID
Infant conjunctival testing requires epithelial cells; nasopharyngeal testing for pneumonia
Sexually active MSM: annual site-specific screening; every 3–6 months with persistent high risk

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Uncomplicated infection → **doxycycline for 7 days**; LGV → 21 days
★ Pregnancy → **azithromycin**, single dose; alternative when adherence doubtful, less reliable for rectal infection
Neonatal disease → oral erythromycin for 14 days; azithromycin alternative; topical treatment alone inadequate
Gonorrhea suspected or detected → add ceftriaxone; PID requires broader multidrug coverage

rows.label: Complications
items: PID → tubal infertility, ectopic pregnancy, chronic pelvic pain; epididymitis, reactive arthritis
LGV → rectal strictures/fistulas; infant macrolides → hypertrophic pyloric stenosis risk

rows.label: Prevention
items: ★ Treat partners from preceding **60 days**; expedited partner treatment where legal
Abstain until 7-day course completed or 7 days after single dose, and partners treated
Annual screening: sexually active women <25 years, older women with risk; pregnancy entry screening, risk-based rescreening
Retest at 3 months; pregnancy test-of-cure at 4 weeks; neonatal eye ointment does not prevent chlamydia

rows.label: Mimics
items: Gonorrhea: often more purulent; organism-specific NAAT differentiates
M. genitalium: persistent nongonococcal urethritis after doxycycline; separate NAAT
HSV: painful ulcers and external dysuria rather than isolated cervical discharge

chromosomal-and-genetic-disorders.name: Chromosomal and genetic disorders
chromosomal-and-genetic-disorders.scope: Down syndrome (trisomy 21), Turner syndrome (45,X0), Klinefelter syndrome (47,XXY), Fragile X syndrome (FMR1 trinucleotide repeat), Prader-Willi and Angelman syndromes, DiGeorge syndrome (22q11 deletion)
chromosomal-and-genetic-disorders.core: Recognize syndromic combinations of growth, cognition, gonadal function, dysmorphism, and congenital malformations; confirm with the correct genetic test.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Advanced maternal age: meiotic nondisjunction; balanced parental translocation: recurrent aneuploid pregnancy
Family expansion history: repeat disorders; many microdeletions and sex-chromosome abnormalities arise de novo

rows.label: Clues
items: ★ **Down**: hypotonia, upslanting fissures, single palmar crease, AV septal defect
DiGeorge: conotruncal defect, cleft palate, absent thymus, hypocalcemic tetany

rows.label: Pathophys
items: ★ **Genomic imprinting**: parent-specific expression; deletion or uniparental disomy can disrupt the active copy
22q11 deletion disrupts pharyngeal pouch development → T-cell deficiency and hypoparathyroidism

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ Suspected Down → **karyotype confirms trisomy 21**; prenatal screening alone never establishes diagnosis
Microarray: microdeletion; targeted repeat analysis: fragile X; methylation testing: imprinting disorders
Down: assess heart, hearing, vision, thyroid; DiGeorge: calcium and lymphocyte subsets

rows.label: Tx
items: Early developmental services, speech support; repair congenital defects
Turner: growth hormone then estrogen/progestin; Klinefelter: testosterone after endocrine assessment
Prader-Willi: supervised food access; Angelman: seizure management; DiGeorge: calcium and infection management

rows.label: Complications
items: Down: duodenal atresia, leukemia, early Alzheimer disease, atlantoaxial instability
Turner: coarctation, bicuspid valve, aortic dissection; Klinefelter: infertility, breast cancer
Prader-Willi: severe obesity; DiGeorge: severe infections and later psychiatric disease

rows.label: Prevention
items: ★ **Genetic counseling**: recurrence depends on nondisjunction, translocation, imprinting mechanism, or repeat expansion
Avoid live vaccines with severe T-cell deficiency; use irradiated blood for profound immunodeficiency

rows.label: Mimics
items: Noonan syndrome: Turner-like habitus with normal chromosomes; either sex
Congenital hypothyroidism: hypotonia and delayed development; abnormal newborn thyroid screen

table.title: Distinctive genotype–phenotype pairs
rows: Short female, webbed neck, streak ovaries
Tall male, small firm testes, gynecomastia

clostridioides-difficile-infection.name: Clostridioides difficile infection
clostridioides-difficile-infection.scope: Antibiotic-associated diarrhea, toxic megacolon, pseudomembranous colitis, NAAT vs EIA stool toxin testing, oral fidaxomicin, oral vancomycin, fulminant colitis
clostridioides-difficile-infection.core: Recent antibiotics or healthcare exposure followed by watery diarrhea suggests toxin-mediated colitis; ileus can conceal fulminant disease.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Clindamycin, fluoroquinolones, cephalosporins; older age, hospitalization, immunosuppression
Prior infection and unnecessary acid suppression increase susceptibility or recurrence

rows.label: Clues
items: Abdominal cramps, fever, leukocytosis; severe disease may cause AKI and hypoalbuminemia
★ **Hypotension, ileus, or megacolon** defines fulminant infection; diarrhea may disappear

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Antibiotic disruption of microbiota permits spore-forming bacilli to proliferate
Toxins damage colonic epithelium → inflammation and pseudomembranes

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ Test **unformed stool** with ≥3 unexplained stools/24 hours; exclude laxative effect
NAAT detects toxigenic genes, not active toxin; positive results can represent colonization
Toxin EIA is less sensitive; multistep GDH/NAAT plus toxin improves clinical specificity
No test of cure; abdominal imaging for distention, toxicity, or suspected perforation

rows.label: Tx
items: Stop inciting antibiotic when possible; replace fluids/electrolytes, avoid antimotility drugs in severe colitis
★ Initial nonfulminant infection: **oral fidaxomicin** preferred; oral vancomycin acceptable, usually 10 days
★ Fulminant: **high-dose oral/NG vancomycin + IV metronidazole**; add rectal vancomycin with ileus
Shock, perforation, worsening organ failure → urgent surgical consultation
Recurrence: fidaxomicin or tapered/pulsed vancomycin; multiple recurrences → screened microbiota-based treatment

rows.label: Complications
items: Toxic megacolon, perforation, sepsis, recurrent infection
Severe classification: WBC >15,000/µL or creatinine ≥1.5 mg/dL; different from fulminant criteria

rows.label: Prevention
items: Contact precautions, gloves/gown, soap-and-water handwashing, sporicidal surface cleaning
Antibiotic stewardship; no screening/treatment of asymptomatic carriers

rows.label: Mimics
items: Laxative-associated diarrhea: medication timing, no inflammatory syndrome
IBD flare: chronic relapsing course; test for coinfection before escalating immunosuppression

congenital-heart-disease.name: Congenital heart disease
congenital-heart-disease.scope: Cyanotic heart disease (5 Ts: Tetralogy of Fallot, TGA, truncus, tricuspid atresia, TAPVR), acyanotic heart disease (VSD, ASD, PDA, coarctation of aorta), hyperoxia test, prostaglandin E1
congenital-heart-disease.core: Neonatal cyanosis or shock as the ductus closes demands urgent assessment for duct-dependent congenital heart disease.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Maternal diabetes, congenital rubella, family history; Down syndrome → AV septal defects
Prematurity → PDA; Turner syndrome → coarctation

rows.label: Clues
items: Poor feeding, diaphoresis, tachypnea, hepatomegaly → infant heart failure
VSD: harsh holosystolic lower-left sternal murmur; ASD: **fixed split S2**
PDA: continuous machinery murmur, bounding pulses; coarctation: weak femoral pulses, arm–leg BP gradient

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Left-to-right shunts increase pulmonary flow; longstanding vascular remodeling can reverse flow → Eisenmenger syndrome
Duct-dependent lesions require pulmonary/systemic flow or mixing through fetal communications

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ Preductal/right-hand and postductal/foot oxygen saturation; **echocardiography** defines anatomy
★ Hyperoxia test: little PaO2 rise with 100% oxygen suggests cardiac shunting; echo preferred
ECG and chest radiograph support diagnosis; normal murmur does not exclude critical disease

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Suspected duct-dependent lesion → **prostaglandin E1** immediately; monitor for apnea
★ Tet spell → knee–chest position, oxygen, fluids, morphine; refractory → phenylephrine or propranolol
TGA with inadequate mixing → balloon atrial septostomy, then arterial switch
Large shunts → diuretics, closure; premature PDA → ibuprofen; **obstructed TAPVR → emergency repair**
Coarctation → repair; irreversible Eisenmenger physiology → **do not close shunt**

rows.label: Complications
items: Pulmonary hypertension, failure to thrive, arrhythmias, infective endocarditis
Right-to-left shunting → brain abscess, paradoxical emboli, secondary erythrocytosis

rows.label: Prevention
items: Pulse-ox newborn screening; rubella immunization before pregnancy; maternal glycemic control
Endocarditis prophylaxis for selected unrepaired cyanotic or prosthetic-material lesions during dental procedures

rows.label: Mimics
items: Lung disease: substantial oxygen response, pulmonary findings
PPHN: elevated pulmonary resistance with structurally normal heart

table.title: Five cyanotic lesions
rows: RV obstruction, VSD, overriding aorta, RVH; boot-shaped heart
Parallel circuits; single S2; egg-on-string silhouette
Pulmonary veins drain systemically; obstruction → edema

congenital-urinary-tract-anomalies.name: Congenital urinary tract anomalies
congenital-urinary-tract-anomalies.scope: Posterior urethral valves (oligohydramnios, palpable bladder, VCUG, ablation), vesicoureteral reflux (hydronephrosis, recurrent UTI), ureteropelvic junction obstruction, cryptorchidism, hypospadias
congenital-urinary-tract-anomalies.core: Prenatal collecting-system dilation, recurrent febrile UTI, or abnormal genital examination requires localization of obstruction, reflux, or disordered development.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Posterior urethral valves occur only in boys; reflux may cluster in families
Cryptorchidism: prematurity, low birth weight; hypospadias: disrupted urethral development

rows.label: Clues
items: ★ Boy with **weak stream, palpable bladder**, bilateral hydronephrosis → outlet obstruction
Severe fetal obstruction → oligohydramnios, pulmonary hypoplasia, Potter sequence
Recurrent febrile UTIs, poor growth, hypertension may signal reflux nephropathy
★ Hypospadias + bilateral nonpalpable testes → urgent disorder-of-sex-development evaluation

rows.label: Pathophys
items: High urinary pressure or retrograde infected urine damages developing renal parenchyma
Undescended testes experience thermal injury; ectopic ventral meatus may accompany chordee

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ Renal/bladder **ultrasound** first; creatinine, electrolytes, urinalysis/culture assess consequences
VCUG after abnormal ultrasound suggesting reflux/obstruction or recurrent febrile UTIs; not every first uncomplicated UTI
UPJ dilation without hydroureter → MAG3 diuretic renography for drainage and differential function
Cryptorchidism: examination; no pre-referral ultrasound; bilateral nonpalpable testes → endocrine/genetic evaluation

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Valves: bladder catheter decompression, correct fluids/electrolytes → endoscopic **valve ablation**
Reflux: low-risk → observation; high-risk → consider TMP-SMX prophylaxis; breakthrough febrile UTIs → ureteral reimplantation
UPJ obstruction: observe preserved function; worsening drainage/function or symptoms → pyeloplasty
Cryptorchidism: refer at 6 months corrected age; orchiopexy by 18 months
★ Hypospadias: **defer circumcision**; foreskin may support reconstruction; repair generally 6–18 months

rows.label: Complications
items: Renal scarring, CKD, hypertension; valve bladder dysfunction may persist after successful ablation
Cryptorchidism: subfertility, torsion, malignancy; orchiopexy reduces but does not eliminate cancer risk

rows.label: Prevention
items: Treat constipation and dysfunctional voiding to reduce recurrent UTIs
Prompt fever evaluation and long-term BP/renal-function surveillance after significant reflux or obstruction

rows.label: Mimics
items: Retractile testis: can remain in scrotum after manipulation; monitor annually for ascent
Physiologic neonatal dilation: resolves without progressive functional loss

croup.name: Croup
croup.scope: Parainfluenza virus, barking cough, inspiratory stridor, hoarseness, steeple sign, Westley score, nebulized epinephrine, dexamethasone
croup.core: A toddler with a viral prodrome develops a barking cough, hoarseness, and inspiratory stridor from subglottic airway narrowing.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Usually 6 months–3 years; parainfluenza most common, other respiratory viruses possible
Autumn/winter exposure, daycare; recurrent or atypical-age episodes suggest structural airway disease

rows.label: Clues
items: Symptoms often worsen at night; low-grade fever, retractions, agitation with respiratory distress
★ **Stridor at rest** marks clinically significant obstruction; cyanosis/lethargy suggests impending failure
Drooling, tripod posture, toxicity, or high fever → reconsider diagnosis

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Viral laryngotracheal inflammation causes edema within the rigid cricoid ring
Small reductions in pediatric airway radius produce large increases in airflow resistance

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **Clinical diagnosis**; routine imaging, viral testing, and blood draws unnecessary
AP neck x-ray: steeple-shaped subglottic narrowing, supportive but neither required nor specific
Westley: stridor, retractions, air entry, cyanosis, consciousness; 0–2 mild, 3–7 moderate, ≥8 severe

rows.label: Tx
items: Keep child calm with caregiver; oxygen if hypoxemic; avoid unnecessary upsetting procedures
★ **Dexamethasone once for all severities**; oral route preferred when tolerated
★ Moderate/severe disease → **nebulized epinephrine**; observe ≥2–3 hours after last dose
Persistent resting symptoms, repeated epinephrine, poor intake → admit; exhaustion/hypoxia → expert airway management
No routine antibiotics, bronchodilators, or cough suppressants; humidified air lacks proven benefit

rows.label: Complications
items: Respiratory failure, dehydration; rare secondary bacterial tracheitis
Epinephrine effect wears off before steroid benefit; reassess rather than discharge immediately

rows.label: Prevention
items: Hand hygiene, respiratory etiquette, reduced close contact during acute viral illness

rows.label: Mimics
items: Epiglottitis: drooling, dysphagia, muffled voice, tripod posture; secure airway without throat manipulation
Bacterial tracheitis: toxic, high fever, thick secretions, poor epinephrine response
Foreign body: abrupt choking, no preceding viral syndrome

dermatophyte-infections.name: Dermatophyte infections
dermatophyte-infections.scope: Tinea capitis, tinea corporis, tinea pedis, tinea cruris, onychomycosis, potassium hydroxide preparation, oral and topical antifungals
dermatophyte-infections.core: Keratin-invading fungi cause scaly skin lesions or infected hair/nails; the anatomic site determines topical versus systemic treatment.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Warm humid conditions, occlusive footwear, shared showers, wrestling, infected animals or contacts
Diabetes, immunosuppression; childhood favors scalp infection; nail disease increases with age

rows.label: Clues
items: Pruritus and peripheral scaling; steroid exposure may distort borders and suppress inflammation
★ **Boggy tender scalp plaque** → kerion; inflammatory disease risks permanent scarring alopecia
Interdigital maceration/fissures can become bacterial entry sites

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Trichophyton, Microsporum, Epidermophyton digest keratin in stratum corneum, hair, and nails
Follicular/deep involvement prevents topical agents from reaching the infected reservoir

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **KOH preparation of active edge** → branching septate hyphae; obtain before systemic treatment when uncertain
Scalp: hair/plucked scale microscopy and culture; nail: clipping KOH, PAS, or fungal culture
Wood lamp detects only selected organisms; negative fluorescence does not exclude tinea
Refractory/widespread infection → reassess diagnosis, adherence, resistance; fungal culture can guide further care

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Limited skin disease → **topical terbinafine** or clotrimazole; continue beyond clinical clearing
★ Hair infection → **oral griseofulvin or terbinafine**; adjunct selenium sulfide/ketoconazole shampoo reduces spread
Nail infection → confirm fungus, then oral terbinafine; baseline liver assessment; counsel slow regrowth
Avoid topical corticosteroid monotherapy or steroid-antifungal combinations; extensive disease may require oral antifungal

rows.label: Complications
items: Secondary cellulitis, persistent nail dystrophy, recurrent infection from untreated reservoirs
Oral antifungals: hepatotoxicity, drug interactions; griseofulvin contraindicated during pregnancy

rows.label: Prevention
items: ★ **Keep feet dry**, change socks, avoid shared towels/combs, disinfect sports gear
Treat symptomatic contacts/pets and coexisting foot disease; avoid barefoot communal-shower exposure

rows.label: Mimics
items: Candida intertrigo: satellite pustules, scrotal involvement
Psoriasis: sharply demarcated plaques, nail pitting; alopecia areata: smooth nonscaly patches

table.title: Site clues
rows: Broken hairs, black dots, patchy alopecia
Annular plaque, advancing border, central clearing
Thick yellow brittle nail, subungual debris

dermatophyte-infections.evidence: Not checked online; established dermatophyte diagnosis and site-based treatment.

esophageal-atresia-and-tracheoesophageal.name: Esophageal atresia and tracheoesophageal fistula
esophageal-atresia-and-tracheoesophageal.scope: Esophageal atresia, tracheoesophageal fistula types, VACTERL association, coiled nasogastric tube on chest x-ray
esophageal-atresia-and-tracheoesophageal.core: A newborn with excessive oral secretions, choking and cyanosis during feeds requires evaluation for esophageal atresia or tracheoesophageal fistula.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Prenatal polyhydramnios and small/absent stomach bubble suggest impaired fetal swallowing
Associated anomalies: **VACTERL**—vertebral, anal, cardiac, tracheoesophageal, renal and limb defects

rows.label: Clues
items: Frothy drooling, feeding-associated respiratory distress, recurrent desaturation or aspiration
★ **Nasogastric/orogastric tube cannot pass** into stomach; avoid repeated forceful attempts
Abdominal distention suggests airway-to-stomach communication; isolated atresia often has gasless abdomen
H-type fistula: esophagus patent, delayed recurrent pneumonia or cough with liquids

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Abnormal foregut separation leaves esophageal discontinuity and/or connection to trachea
Secretions pool proximally; distal communication permits reflux aspiration and gastric inflation during ventilation

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ Gentle radiopaque tube placement → **chest/abdominal radiograph showing proximal coiling**
Distal bowel gas supports distal fistula; absent gas favors no distal connection
Routine contrast feeding unnecessary in classic atresia; aspiration can worsen lung injury
Suspected H-type → carefully supervised contrast esophagram and bronchoscopy
Echocardiography before surgery; assess anus, kidneys, spine and limbs for associated anomalies

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ **NPO, head elevation, continuous proximal pouch suction**, IV fluids and pediatric surgical referral
Secure airway if respiratory failure; minimize bag-mask ventilation because fistula can inflate stomach
★ Definitive → **fistula ligation and esophageal anastomosis** after stabilization
Long-gap atresia → staged nutritional and reconstructive plan; aspiration pneumonia → IV antibiotics
Feeding resumed after postoperative assessment of repair integrity and swallowing safety

rows.label: Complications
items: Aspiration pneumonia, anastomotic leak/stricture, recurrent fistula, reflux and dysmotility
Associated tracheomalacia can cause persistent noisy breathing, cyanotic spells or recurrent respiratory infection

rows.label: Prevention
items: Prenatal recognition enables delivery planning; aspiration precautions until repaired
Long-term monitoring for dysphagia, reflux, growth failure and recurrent respiratory symptoms

rows.label: Mimics
items: Choanal atresia: cyanosis improves with crying; nasal catheter obstructed
Laryngeal cleft: aspiration with patent esophagus
Pyloric stenosis: later nonbilious vomiting without tube coiling

table.title: Anatomic patterns
rows: Most common; proximal pouch + bowel gas

gastroesophageal-reflux-disease.name: Gastroesophageal reflux disease
gastroesophageal-reflux-disease.scope: Clinical diagnosis, empiric PPI trial, lifestyle measures, alarm symptoms, Barrett esophagus screening, 24-hour pH monitoring
gastroesophageal-reflux-disease.core: Heartburn and acid regurgitation after meals or recumbency suggest reflux; complications or diagnostic uncertainty change the testing pathway.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Obesity, pregnancy, hiatal hernia, smoking; drugs reducing lower esophageal sphincter tone
Late large meals and individual food triggers exacerbate symptoms

rows.label: Clues
items: Sour taste, nocturnal symptoms, chest discomfort; chronic cough/hoarseness nonspecific and often multifactorial
★ **Dysphagia, odynophagia, bleeding, weight loss**, persistent vomiting, anemia → endoscopy
Exertional or acute chest pain requires cardiac evaluation before attributing symptoms to reflux

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Transient lower sphincter relaxation and impaired barrier allow gastric contents into esophagus
Acid exposure → erosions; chronic injury may produce intestinal metaplasia

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ Typical symptoms without alarms → **8-week empiric once-daily PPI trial**
Alarm features or failed treatment → upper endoscopy; biopsies evaluate alternative mucosal disease
★ Unproven GERD + normal endoscopy → **ambulatory pH monitoring off PPI**
Proven GERD with refractory symptoms → impedance-pH testing on PPI after optimizing use
Manometry evaluates motility and precedes antireflux surgery; not the primary reflux diagnostic test

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ **Omeprazole 30–60 minutes before breakfast**; verify adherence before escalation
Intermittent mild symptoms → antacid or famotidine; persistent breakthrough → optimize/split PPI schedule
Weight reduction if overweight; avoid meals within 2–3 hours of bedtime, elevate bed head
Objective reflux with troublesome regurgitation despite optimized drugs → fundoplication or selected endoscopic intervention
Severe erosive esophagitis → long-term PPI or surgery; step down uncomplicated controlled disease

rows.label: Complications
items: Erosive esophagitis, peptic stricture, Barrett esophagus, adenocarcinoma
Stricture → endoscopic dilation plus acid suppression; dysplastic Barrett requires specialist eradication treatment

rows.label: Prevention
items: Barrett screening: chronic reflux + ≥3 additional risks: male, >50, White, tobacco, obesity, first-degree family history
Smoking cessation and symptom-directed trigger reduction; routine endoscopy unnecessary for every reflux patient

rows.label: Mimics
items: Achalasia: solids and liquids dysphagia, impaired sphincter relaxation
Eosinophilic esophagitis: atopy, food impaction, eosinophilic biopsy
Functional heartburn: normal reflux burden and no symptom association

gastroesophageal-reflux-disease.evidence: Not checked online; established ACG reflux and Barrett screening teaching.

glomerulonephritis.name: Glomerulonephritis
glomerulonephritis.scope: Nephritic syndrome, poststreptococcal GN, IgA nephropathy, rapidly progressive GN (anti-GBM, ANCA), lupus nephritis, RBC casts and dysmorphic RBCs, proteinuria quantification, kidney biopsy
glomerulonephritis.core: Glomerular inflammation causes hematuria, proteinuria, hypertension, edema, and reduced filtration; rapidly rising creatinine demands urgent evaluation for crescentic disease.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Recent streptococcal pharyngitis/skin infection, systemic autoimmunity, small-vessel vasculitis
IgA nephropathy often follows mucosal infection; anti-GBM pulmonary bleeding risk increases with smoking

rows.label: Clues
items: ★ **RBC casts and dysmorphic RBCs** identify a glomerular bleeding source
Tea-colored urine, oliguria, periorbital swelling; nephrotic-range protein loss can coexist
★ **Hemoptysis + AKI** → pulmonary–renal syndrome; rapidly progressive disease may initially lack systemic symptoms

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Immune complexes, basement-membrane antibodies, or pauci-immune vascular injury inflame glomerular capillaries
Crescent formation compresses capillary tufts → rapid, potentially irreversible loss of filtration

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ Urinalysis/microscopy → **creatinine, electrolytes, urine protein/creatinine ratio**; monitor urine output
C3/C4, ANA/dsDNA, ANCA, anti-GBM; ASO/anti-DNase B when poststreptococcal disease suspected
★ **Kidney biopsy** for rapidly progressive AKI, substantial persistent proteinuria, or uncertain systemic GN
Typical childhood poststreptococcal course may not require biopsy; persistent low C3 beyond 8 weeks warrants reassessment

rows.label: Tx
items: Salt restriction, loop diuretics for overload, BP control; ACE inhibitor/ARB for persistent proteinuria when stable
★ Pulmonary–renal/RPGN → **urgent nephrology, steroids + immunosuppression** before irreversible decline
Anti-GBM: plasma exchange + cyclophosphamide; ANCA: rituximab/cyclophosphamide; plasma exchange only selected severe cases
Lupus: biopsy-directed mycophenolate/cyclophosphamide + steroids; poststreptococcal disease mainly supportive

rows.label: Complications
items: Hyperkalemia, pulmonary edema, hypertensive emergency, CKD; dialysis for refractory life-threatening derangements
Immunosuppression → infection, cytopenias, infertility with cyclophosphamide

rows.label: Prevention
items: Control BP/proteinuria, avoid nephrotoxins, follow renal function and urine findings

rows.label: Mimics
items: ATN: muddy-brown casts after ischemia/toxins
Urologic bleeding: isomorphic RBCs, clots, no RBC casts

glomerulonephritis.evidence: Not checked online; established nephrology teaching.

hirsutism.name: Hirsutism
hirsutism.scope: Idiopathic hirsutism, peripheral 5-alpha-reductase overactivity, evaluation of androgen excess, nonclassic CAH, androgen-secreting neoplasms, oral contraceptives, spironolactone
hirsutism.core: Terminal hair in androgen-dependent areas in women requires distinguishing gradual androgen sensitivity/PCOS from rapid virilization due to a secreting tumor.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: PCOS, familial/ethnic hair distribution, nonclassic CAH, exogenous androgens/anabolic steroids
Rare ovarian/adrenal neoplasm; medications causing generalized hypertrichosis differ from androgenic hair growth

rows.label: Clues
items: Facial, chest, lower-abdominal terminal hair; acne and irregular menses favor androgen excess
★ **Rapid progression, deep voice, clitoromegaly**, increased muscle mass → tumor evaluation
Regular ovulatory cycles with normal androgens and slow growth favor idiopathic hirsutism

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Androgens convert vellus to terminal hairs; follicular 5-alpha-reductase converts testosterone to potent DHT
Idiopathic disease reflects increased peripheral sensitivity despite normal circulating hormones

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ Moderate/severe hair growth or endocrine signs → morning **total testosterone**, reliable assay
DHEA-S assesses adrenal source; early-morning follicular **17-hydroxyprogesterone** screens nonclassic CAH
Marked testosterone elevation, often >150–200 ng/dL → pelvic imaging; DHEA-S >700 µg/dL → adrenal imaging
Equivocal 17-hydroxyprogesterone → ACTH stimulation; TSH/prolactin or cortisol testing only for matching features
Mild localized hair without abnormal cycles/endocrine signs often needs no extensive hormone workup

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Pregnancy not desired → **combined OCP** first-line; reassess after ≥6 months
★ Persistent symptoms → add **spironolactone with reliable contraception**; monitor potassium/renal function
Shaving, waxing, laser/photoepilation; topical eflornithine slows facial hair growth
Treat tumor/endocrine cause; weight loss benefits metabolic risk and androgen excess in PCOS

rows.label: Complications
items: Psychological distress; spironolactone → hyperkalemia, menstrual irregularity, male fetal undervirilization
Estrogen contraception → VTE risk; avoid when estrogen contraindicated

rows.label: Prevention
items: Avoid androgen supplements; counsel slow hair-cycle response and ongoing maintenance

rows.label: Mimics
items: Hypertrichosis: diffuse nonandrogen distribution; minoxidil, phenytoin, cyclosporine
Cushing syndrome: striae, proximal weakness, easy bruising accompany hair changes

hirsutism.evidence: Treatment checked 2026-10-30: [SOGC 444](https://www.sogc.org/common/Uploaded%20files/ACSC/ACSC2024/gui444CPG2312E.pdf); biochemical localization established endocrine teaching.

humeral-fractures.name: Humeral fractures
humeral-fractures.scope: Proximal humerus fracture (axillary nerve), humeral shaft fracture (radial nerve, wrist drop), neurologic assessment, coaptation splint, functional brace, surgical fixation indications
humeral-fractures.core: Humeral fracture management depends on location, displacement, and neurovascular injury; document nerve function before and after manipulation.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Older adults with osteoporosis: low-energy proximal fractures; younger adults: high-energy trauma
Shaft injuries from direct blow, twisting, falls; consider malignancy with minimal-trauma shaft fracture

rows.label: Clues
items: Upper-arm pain, swelling, ecchymosis, deformity; reduced shoulder/elbow motion
★ Proximal/surgical neck injury → **axillary nerve**: lateral shoulder numbness, impaired deltoid function
★ Shaft injury → **radial nerve**: wrist/finger extension weakness, dorsal first-web-space sensory loss
Cold pulseless hand, expanding hematoma, severe stretch pain → urgent vascular/compartment evaluation

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Axillary nerve wraps around surgical neck; radial nerve travels along the spiral groove
Closed-fracture radial palsy often reflects neurapraxia and recovers without immediate exploration

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **AP/lateral humerus radiographs including shoulder and elbow**; dedicated joint views when involved
Check pulses, capillary refill, motor/sensory function of radial, median, ulnar, and axillary nerves
Repeat examination after reduction/splinting; CT for complex proximal/articular fracture planning
Open wound near fracture → evaluate as open fracture even if bone not visible

rows.label: Tx
items: Analgesia, immobilization, ice; open injury → IV cefazolin, tetanus protection, urgent irrigation/debridement
★ Most closed shaft fractures → **coaptation splint**, then functional brace after swelling subsides
Minimally displaced proximal fracture → sling, early supervised range of motion to limit stiffness
Displaced complex proximal patterns → fixation or selected arthroplasty depending on age and reconstructability
★ Surgery: **open fracture, vascular injury, floating elbow**, unacceptable alignment, failed bracing/nonunion

rows.label: Complications
items: Radial nerve palsy, malunion/nonunion; proximal injuries: avascular necrosis, shoulder stiffness
Secondary/new palsy after reduction or penetrating injury → urgent specialist reassessment, possible exploration

rows.label: Prevention
items: Fall reduction, osteoporosis evaluation after fragility fracture; rehabilitation preserves joint motion
No prolonged unmonitored sling use; regular alignment and neurovascular follow-up

rows.label: Mimics
items: Shoulder dislocation: altered contour and displaced humeral head on joint views
Rotator cuff tear: weakness without fracture, especially persistent after healing

humeral-fractures.evidence: Not checked online; established orthopedic teaching.

hyperbilirubinemia.name: Hyperbilirubinemia
hyperbilirubinemia.scope: Gilbert syndrome, Crigler-Najjar, Dubin-Johnson, Rotor, unconjugated vs conjugated, biliary atresia
hyperbilirubinemia.core: Fractionate bilirubin first: indirect elevation reflects production or conjugation problems; direct elevation requires assessment of hepatobiliary excretion.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Fasting, illness or dehydration triggers Gilbert jaundice; family history suggests inherited bilirubin disorders
Persistent infant jaundice can reflect biliary atresia even after initially reassuring appearance

rows.label: Clues
items: Indirect bilirubin is albumin-bound and absent from urine; direct bilirubin can darken urine
★ Infant **pale/acholic stools**, dark urine, hepatomegaly → obstructive cholestasis
Pruritus, pale stools and elevated alkaline phosphatase suggest impaired bile flow
Severe neonatal indirect elevation with lethargy, poor feeding or abnormal tone → bilirubin neurotoxicity

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Heme breakdown yields unconjugated pigment; hepatic UGT conjugation enables biliary elimination
Unbound unconjugated bilirubin crosses the immature blood–brain barrier; conjugated bilirubin does not cause kernicterus

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **Total/direct bilirubin**, AST/ALT, alkaline phosphatase/GGT; CBC/reticulocytes/LDH for suspected hemolysis
Isolated mild indirect elevation with normal liver tests and no hemolysis → Gilbert diagnosis
★ Jaundice beyond 2 weeks → fractionate; **direct ≥1 mg/dL at 2–4 weeks** → urgent referral
Infant cholestasis → ultrasound; biliary atresia assessment may require biopsy and operative cholangiography
Adult conjugated elevation with pain/obstruction → RUQ ultrasound before advanced duct imaging

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Suspected biliary atresia → urgent pediatric hepatology/surgery; **early Kasai portoenterostomy**
Severe neonatal indirect elevation → age/gestation/risk-based phototherapy; exchange transfusion at critical thresholds
Crigler–Najjar I → intensive phototherapy, definitive liver transplant; type II responds to phenobarbital
Gilbert, Dubin–Johnson and Rotor → reassurance once competing pathology excluded
Cholestasis → nutritional support, fat-soluble vitamins and cause-specific treatment

rows.label: Complications
items: Indirect neonatal hyperbilirubinemia → acute encephalopathy/kernicterus
Untreated atresia → cirrhosis, portal hypertension, liver failure

rows.label: Prevention
items: ★ Inspect stool color and fractionate persistent infant jaundice; never label conjugated jaundice physiologic

rows.label: Mimics
items: Hemolysis: anemia, reticulocytosis, low haptoglobin
Choledochal cyst: cystic/dilated extrahepatic ducts on ultrasound

hyperbilirubinemia.evidence: Infant referral checked 2026-10-30: [AAP 2025](https://publications.aap.org/aapnews/news/pdfDownload/31302); inherited syndromes established teaching.

hyperglycemic-crises.name: Hyperglycemic crises
hyperglycemic-crises.core: Insulin-deficient diabetes with osmotic diuresis: rapid acidotic illness or slowly progressive hyperosmolar encephalopathy.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Infection, missed insulin, pump failure, MI; DKA often type 1, HHS often older type 2
Euglycemic triggers: **SGLT2 inhibitors**, pregnancy, fasting

rows.label: Clues
items: Polyuria, thirst, weight loss, dry mucosa, tachycardia
DKA: abdominal pain, vomiting, **Kussmaul breathing**; HHS: profound dehydration, focal deficits
★ Severe: **hypotension, stupor**, or coma → ICU

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Insulin deficit + counterregulatory hormones → lipolysis, ketogenesis; residual insulin in HHS limits ketosis
Total-body K depleted despite initially normal/high serum K

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **Glucose, electrolytes, venous pH, β-hydroxybutyrate**, osmolality; ECG + trigger evaluation
Effective osmolality = 2 × Na + glucose/18; glucose in mg/dL
★ HHS: **effective osmolality >300 OR total >320 mOsm/kg**; substantial ketosis/acidosis → mixed DKA/HHS
DKA resolution: ketones <0.6 mmol/L AND (pH ≥7.3 OR HCO₃ ≥18); urine ketones/anion gap misleading

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ **IV isotonic crystalloid → K correction → IV regular insulin**; K <3.5 mmol/L → delay insulin
Replace K when <5 mmol/L; glucose checks every 1–2 h, electrolytes/pH/ketones every 4 h
★ Add **dextrose** below glucose 250; euglycemic presentation → immediately; continue insulin until crisis resolves
SC basal insulin overlaps infusion 1–2 h; bicarbonate only consider pH <7.0; HHS: slower osmolar correction

rows.label: Complications
items: AKI, thrombosis; treatment: hypoglycemia, hypokalemic arrhythmias, cerebral edema, hyperchloremic acidosis

rows.label: Prevention
items: Sick-day fluids/ketone checks; continue basal insulin; ensure supplies and early follow-up
Hold SGLT2 inhibitors during acute illness and before surgery

rows.label: Mimics
items: Alcoholic ketoacidosis: binge then poor intake; usually no diabetes
Starvation ketosis: usually milder acidosis, no marked hyperglycemia
Toxic alcohols: osmolar gap, exposure; absent substantial ketonemia
