hypertensive-crises.name: Hypertensive crises
hypertensive-crises.scope: Hypertensive urgency, hypertensive emergency, hypertensive encephalopathy, aortic dissection, acute pulmonary edema, IV labetalol, nicardipine, nitroprusside
hypertensive-crises.core: Severe BP elevation becomes an emergency when new target-organ injury accompanies it; the number alone does not determine urgency.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Missed antihypertensives, CKD, sympathomimetics; clonidine withdrawal
Pregnancy, renovascular disease, catecholamine excess

rows.label: Clues
items: ★ Usually **>180/120 mm Hg** with AKI, ACS, pulmonary edema, stroke, or dissection
Encephalopathy: headache, confusion, seizures, visual disturbance; papilledema or retinal hemorrhages

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Autoregulatory failure → endothelial injury, microangiopathy, tissue ischemia; cerebral vasogenic edema in PRES

rows.label: Dx
items: Repeat correctly sized cuff reading; examine neurologic status, fundi, pulses, heart and lungs
Creatinine, electrolytes, urinalysis, ECG; troponin with cardiac symptoms
Neurologic symptoms → head CT; suspected dissection → CTA chest/aorta
MRI posterior vasogenic edema supports PRES after hemorrhage exclusion

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Most emergencies: ICU, titratable IV **nicardipine or labetalol**
★ Reduce MAP ≤25% first hour → approximately 160/100–110 over 2–6 hours; then gradual normalization
★ No acute injury: treat pain/anxiety, restart or adjust oral drugs, arrange close outpatient follow-up
Avoid rapid IV lowering for asymptomatic BP; avoid immediate-release nifedipine
Nitroprusside: cyanide/thiocyanate toxicity with prolonged use or renal/hepatic dysfunction; monitor closely

rows.label: Complications
items: Cerebral hemorrhage, renal failure, MI; overly rapid lowering → cerebral/coronary hypoperfusion

rows.label: Prevention
items: Medication access and adherence; home BP monitoring; avoid cocaine and amphetamines

rows.label: Mimics
items: Pain/anxiety elevation: improves after trigger control, no acute injury
Ischemic stroke: permissive hypertension thresholds differ; avoid applying generic reduction targets

hypertrophic-pyloric-stenosis.name: Hypertrophic Pyloric Stenosis
hypertrophic-pyloric-stenosis.scope: infantile presentation (nonbilious projectile vomiting, olive mass), hypochloremic hypokalemic metabolic alkalosis, ultrasound diagnosis, fluid resuscitation, pyloromyotomy
hypertrophic-pyloric-stenosis.core: A hungry young infant with progressive projectile nonbilious vomiting suggests gastric outlet obstruction from pyloric muscle hypertrophy.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Usually 2–8 weeks old; more common in firstborn boys and with family history
Early-life macrolide exposure, especially erythromycin; bottle feeding and maternal smoking associated

rows.label: Clues
items: Vomiting becomes forceful after feeds; dehydration, weight loss, fewer wet diapers
★ **Palpable epigastric/right-upper-quadrant olive**, visible left-to-right gastric peristalsis
★ **Hypochloremic, hypokalemic metabolic alkalosis** after prolonged vomiting; labs may initially be normal
Bilious emesis is atypical and demands urgent evaluation for obstruction distal to ampulla

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Hypertrophied pyloric circular muscle obstructs gastric emptying without blocking bile drainage into distal bowel
Gastric HCl loss and contraction activate aldosterone → renal potassium loss; severe depletion causes paradoxical aciduria

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **Ultrasound first**: thickened elongated pylorus with impaired passage
Typical thresholds: muscle thickness ≥3 mm, channel length ≥15 mm; interpret by infant size
Equivocal early study → repeat ultrasound; upper GI series can show string sign if uncertainty persists
Electrolytes, glucose, renal function, blood gas assess resuscitation needs before anesthesia

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ **NPO + IV isotonic saline**, glucose-containing maintenance fluid; correct chloride deficit first
Replace potassium after confirming urine output; monitor hydration and electrolytes
★ **Pyloromyotomy after normalization** of volume and alkalosis; medical stabilization precedes definitive surgery
NG decompression when ongoing vomiting/distention; postoperative feeds advanced with surgical team

rows.label: Complications
items: Severe dehydration, failure to thrive, prerenal AKI, hypokalemic arrhythmia
Persistent alkalosis increases perioperative apnea risk; surgery can cause mucosal perforation or incomplete myotomy
Brief postoperative emesis can occur; persistent worsening vomiting warrants reassessment

rows.label: Prevention
items: No reliable primary prevention; avoid unnecessary neonatal macrolides, without withholding necessary treatment
Early recognition of progressive vomiting prevents severe electrolyte depletion

rows.label: Mimics
items: Physiologic reflux: effortless small spit-ups, normal growth
Malrotation/volvulus: bilious vomiting, acute illness; urgent upper GI evaluation/surgery
Milk-protein allergy: bloody stools, eczema, feeding intolerance rather than fixed outlet obstruction

hypertrophic-pyloric-stenosis.evidence: Not checked online; established pediatric surgery teaching.

hypothyroidism.name: Hypothyroidism
hypothyroidism.scope: Hashimoto thyroiditis, subclinical hypothyroidism, myxedema coma, autoimmune associations, levothyroxine dosing, TSH monitoring
hypothyroidism.core: Insufficient thyroid hormone slows metabolism, causing fatigue, cold intolerance, constipation, dry skin, and delayed reflex relaxation.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Hashimoto autoimmunity, thyroid surgery/radioiodine, iodine deficiency/excess
Lithium, amiodarone, postpartum thyroiditis; pituitary surgery/radiation or mass

rows.label: Clues
items: Weight gain, bradycardia, hoarseness, heavy menses, hyperlipidemia; hyponatremia in severe disease
★ **Hypothermia, altered mentation, hypoventilation, hypotension** → myxedema coma
Autoimmune clustering: type 1 diabetes, pernicious anemia, adrenal insufficiency, celiac disease

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Reduced hormone activity lowers thermogenesis and cardiac output; glycosaminoglycan deposition produces nonpitting edema
Hashimoto: lymphocytic destruction; anti-TPO antibodies support autoimmune cause

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **TSH and free T4** establish hormone deficiency and localize the level of dysfunction
Positive anti-TPO predicts progression from subclinical disease; ultrasound unnecessary without nodule/goiter concern
Recheck mild isolated TSH elevation after transient illness resolves; exclude medication interference

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ **Levothyroxine**; healthy young adult approximately 1.6 mcg/kg/day; older/CAD start 12.5–25 mcg/day
Take fasting; separate calcium/iron; reassess TSH about 6–8 weeks after changes
Central disease: titrate using free T4; evaluate/replace cortisol before thyroid hormone
Subclinical: generally treat TSH ≥10; consider symptoms, antibodies, pregnancy at lower values
★ Myxedema: **IV levothyroxine + IV hydrocortisone**, airway support, cautious fluids/passive warming; treat trigger

rows.label: Complications
items: Dyslipidemia, infertility, pericardial effusion, neuropathy; severe disease → respiratory failure
Excess replacement → AF, angina, bone loss; rapid correction in CAD can precipitate ischemia

rows.label: Prevention
items: ★ Pregnancy: early **TSH monitoring**, usually increase existing replacement promptly; use pregnancy-specific targets
Monitor stable replacement at least annually; address adherence/absorption before escalating doses

rows.label: Mimics
items: Depression: mood symptoms without thyroid biochemical pattern
Euthyroid sick syndrome: acute systemic illness, often low T3; avoid routine hormone replacement

hypothyroidism.evidence: Not checked online; established thyroid replacement and endocrine emergency teaching.

increased-intracranial-pressure.name: Increased intracranial pressure
increased-intracranial-pressure.scope: Cushing triad, papilledema, ventriculoperitoneal shunt malfunction, idiopathic intracranial hypertension, herniation syndromes, hyperosmolar therapy
increased-intracranial-pressure.core: Progressive headache, vomiting, or depressed consciousness from raised intracranial pressure requires rapid distinction between mass effect, hydrocephalus, and idiopathic intracranial hypertension.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Trauma, intracranial bleeding, tumor, cerebral edema, CNS infection, obstructed CSF flow
VP shunt: blockage or infection; IIH: obesity, reproductive-age women, tetracyclines, retinoids

rows.label: Clues
items: Morning/Valsalva headache, papilledema, diplopia from sixth-nerve palsy; infants may have bulging fontanelle
★ **Cushing triad**: hypertension/widened pulse pressure, bradycardia, irregular respirations; late dangerous finding
Uncal herniation → ipsilateral fixed dilated pupil, contralateral weakness; tonsillar herniation → respiratory arrest
IIH: pulsatile tinnitus, transient visual obscurations; shunt failure: recurrent headache, vomiting, lethargy

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Fixed skull volume: excess tissue, blood, or CSF raises pressure after compensatory reserve exhausted
Cerebral perfusion pressure = MAP − ICP; falling perfusion worsens ischemia and edema

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ Unstable/acute deficit → **noncontrast head CT**; papilledema with stable suspected IIH → MRI + MRV
★ **No LP before excluding mass effect/obstructive hydrocephalus** when concerning signs present
IIH: normal imaging aside from supportive findings, normal CSF composition, opening pressure ≥25 cm H₂O
Shunt failure → head imaging, shunt series, urgent neurosurgery; normal ventricular size does not exclude obstruction

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Herniation concern → **airway support, head elevation, IV hypertonic saline or mannitol**, urgent neurosurgery
Avoid hypoxia/hypotension; brief controlled hyperventilation only as bridge for impending herniation
Hydrocephalus → CSF drainage/shunt revision; mass lesion → definitive decompression
Dexamethasone for tumor-associated vasogenic edema; no corticosteroids for traumatic brain injury
IIH → weight loss + acetazolamide; threatened vision → optic nerve fenestration or CSF diversion

rows.label: Complications
items: Permanent visual loss, ischemic injury, herniation, death
Hyperosmolar agents → electrolyte/renal disturbances; CSF devices → infection

rows.label: Prevention
items: Avoid causative drugs in IIH; follow visual fields and optic discs
Shunt education: prompt evaluation for recurrence or fever; injury prevention

rows.label: Mimics
items: Migraine: normal fundus and no progressive focal/mental-status findings
Cerebral venous thrombosis: venous obstruction on MRV, not idiopathic disease

increased-intracranial-pressure.evidence: Not checked online; established neurocritical care and IIH diagnostic principles.

intussusception.name: Intussusception
intussusception.scope: Idiopathic ileocolic intussusception, pathologic lead points (Meckel, polyp), target sign on ultrasound, air enema
intussusception.core: Bowel telescoping causes intermittent obstruction and ischemia, often in a previously healthy infant with episodic distress and deceptively well intervals.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Usually age 6–36 months; lymphoid hyperplasia after viral illness
Older child, recurrent episode or adult → pathologic lead point: Meckel diverticulum, polyp, lymphoma

rows.label: Clues
items: ★ Sudden recurrent **colicky pain with knees drawn up**, pallor and vomiting
Lethargy can dominate; bilious emesis or distention suggests progressing obstruction
Sausage-shaped RUQ mass, empty RLQ; currant-jelly stool is late and often absent
Shock, guarding, fever or peritonitis → compromised bowel/perforation

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Proximal bowel and mesentery invaginate distally → venous congestion, edema and arterial ischemia
Ileocolic location most common in children; bleeding reflects injured mucosa

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **Abdominal ultrasound first** → target/doughnut on transverse view, pseudokidney longitudinally
Plain radiograph for obstruction/free air when severe findings; normal radiograph does not exclude
CT generally for adult cases or uncertain alternative diagnosis, not routine pediatric first test
Classic clinical triad uncommon; do not delay testing until bloody stools appear

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ **NPO, IV fluids**, analgesia; NG decompression for significant vomiting/distention
★ Stable without peritonitis/perforation → **air or contrast enema reduction** with surgical backup
Failed reduction, perforation, shock or peritonitis → urgent surgery; resect nonviable bowel
Persistent/recurrent disease or suspected lead point → surgical evaluation; adult cases usually require resection

rows.label: Complications
items: Bowel necrosis, perforation, sepsis, shock; recurrence after successful reduction
Enema-associated perforation → immediate surgical management

rows.label: Prevention
items: No usual primary prevention for idiopathic disease; remove identified pathologic lead point
After reduction → observe recovery, resume intake when tolerated; counsel on recurrent episodic symptoms

rows.label: Mimics
items: Gastroenteritis: diarrhea predominates, less discrete symptom-free intervals
Malrotation/volvulus: bilious vomiting in neonate, urgent surgical evaluation

lymphoma.name: Lymphoma
lymphoma.scope: Hodgkin lymphoma (Reed-Sternberg cells, CD15/CD30, B symptoms, mediastinal mass), non-Hodgkin lymphoma (diffuse large B-cell, follicular, Burkitt, mantle cell), Ann Arbor staging, excisional lymph node biopsy
lymphoma.core: Persistent painless lymphadenopathy, splenomegaly, or constitutional symptoms require tissue diagnosis; lymphoma subtype determines urgency, staging, and treatment.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: EBV, HIV, transplantation/immunosuppression; autoimmune disease and older age for many NHL subtypes
Hodgkin incidence peaks in young adults and older age

rows.label: Clues
items: ★ **B symptoms**: unexplained fever >38 °C, drenching night sweats, >10% weight loss in 6 months
Rubbery nodes; NHL often noncontiguous/extranodal; bulky thoracic disease may cause airway or SVC obstruction
Rapidly enlarging mass, cytopenias, high LDH → aggressive disease; mediastinal disease may obstruct airway/SVC

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Clonal lymphocyte proliferation; most NHLs are B-cell derived
Classical Hodgkin: sparse malignant cells within a reactive inflammatory background

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **Excisional lymph-node biopsy** preserves architecture; core if excision unsafe; FNA alone generally insufficient
Histology, immunophenotyping/flow cytometry, selected cytogenetics classify disease; PET/CT stages FDG-avid lymphoma
Ann Arbor: I one region; II same diaphragm side; III both sides; IV disseminated extranodal disease
CBC, CMP, LDH, uric acid; HIV/HBV/HCV testing before systemic treatment
Stable before biopsy → avoid glucocorticoids obscuring histology; life-threatening compression → urgent specialist management

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Early classical HL → **ABVD ± involved-site radiation**; advanced disease → nivolumab-AVD among current options
DLBCL → rituximab-based combination, commonly R-CHOP; Burkitt → urgent intensive chemotherapy with CNS-directed treatment
Asymptomatic low-burden follicular disease → observation; symptomatic/bulky disease → anti-CD20-based treatment
★ Assess tumor-lysis risk before cytotoxic treatment; hydration and **urate-lowering prophylaxis** when risk warrants

rows.label: Complications
items: Tumor lysis, marrow failure, infection, cord compression, superior vena cava syndrome
Doxorubicin → cardiomyopathy; bleomycin → lung toxicity; later infertility/secondary cancers

rows.label: Prevention
items: Anti-CD20 plus HBsAg+ or anti-HBc+ → entecavir/tenofovir prophylaxis; fertility preservation before chemotherapy
Survivorship care: cardiovascular risk, thyroid/breast surveillance after relevant radiation exposures

rows.label: Mimics
items: Reactive nodes: tender, infection-linked, regress after illness
TB lymphadenitis: granulomatous inflammation; microbiologic confirmation
Leukemia: circulating blasts or marked blood-count abnormalities; marrow evaluation

microcytic-anemia.name: Microcytic anemia
microcytic-anemia.scope: Iron deficiency, anemia of chronic disease, thalassemia, sideroblastic anemia
microcytic-anemia.core: Low hemoglobin with MCV <80 fL: distinguish depleted iron, inflammatory iron sequestration, globin underproduction, and defective heme synthesis.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Menstrual/GI blood loss, pregnancy, low intake, malabsorption → iron depletion
Chronic infection, autoimmune disease, malignancy → inflammatory anemia
Inherited hemoglobin disorders; alcohol, lead, isoniazid, myelodysplasia → disordered heme production

rows.label: Clues
items: Fatigue, pallor, exertional dyspnea; severe anemia → tachycardia, angina, syncope
Pica, koilonychia, restless legs suggest iron deficiency
Markedly low MCV with relatively preserved hemoglobin and high RBC count suggests thalassemia trait

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Inflammation → ↑hepcidin → ferroportin suppression, impaired absorption and iron release
Sideroblasts: mitochondrial iron accumulation in erythroblasts from impaired protoporphyrin synthesis

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **CBC/smear → ferritin**, iron, TIBC, transferrin saturation; ferritin rises with inflammation
★ Ferritin **<45 ng/mL in anemia** supports iron deficiency; normal result cannot exclude during inflammation
★ Adult men/postmenopausal women with iron deficiency → **EGD + colonoscopy**; consider celiac testing
Hemoglobin electrophoresis for suspected beta-thalassemia; alpha trait may require genetic testing; exposure → blood lead

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Iron deficiency → **oral ferrous sulfate**; intolerance/malabsorption or rapid replacement need → IV iron
Treat bleeding source; continue iron about 3 months beyond hemoglobin normalization; reassess nonresponse
Inflammatory anemia → treat underlying disease; selected CKD → iron ± erythropoietin
Sideroblastic: remove trigger, pyridoxine if isoniazid-related; severe thalassemia → transfusion/chelation

rows.label: Complications
items: Iron deficiency: developmental effects in children, adverse pregnancy outcomes
Repeated transfusion → iron overload, cardiac/hepatic injury; oral iron → constipation, dark stool

rows.label: Prevention
items: Adequate dietary iron, pregnancy supplementation, lead-exposure reduction
★ **No empiric long-term iron for thalassemia trait** without documented deficiency

rows.label: Mimics
items: Acute blood loss: initially normocytic; hemoglobin may lag volume loss
Hemolysis: reticulocytosis, ↑LDH/indirect bilirubin, ↓haptoglobin

microcytic-anemia.evidence: Checked 2026-10-30: [AGA iron deficiency evaluation 2020](https://gastro.org/clinical-guidance/gastrointestinal-evaluation-of-iron-deficiency-anemia/); remaining hematology established teaching.

myocarditis.name: Myocarditis
myocarditis.scope: Viral myocarditis, postviral heart failure, elevated cardiac biomarkers, ECG changes, cardiac MRI, supportive heart failure therapy
myocarditis.core: New chest pain, arrhythmia or heart failure after a viral syndrome raises concern for inflammatory myocardial injury.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Recent viral illness, autoimmune disease, immune checkpoint inhibitors and selected drug hypersensitivity
Chagas exposure and giant-cell/eosinophilic disorders matter in selected epidemiologic or fulminant presentations

rows.label: Clues
items: Fatigue, dyspnea, chest discomfort, palpitations; tachycardia disproportionate to fever
Troponin elevation, nonspecific ST–T abnormalities, ventricular ectopy; normal initial studies do not exclude
★ Syncope, sustained ventricular arrhythmia, high-grade AV block or shock → **high-risk myocarditis**
Concurrent pericarditis may produce pleuritic positional pain and diffuse ST elevation

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Direct injury and immune-mediated inflammation damage cardiomyocytes → edema, necrosis and ventricular dysfunction
Residual scar creates an arrhythmic substrate even when systolic function improves

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ ECG, troponin, BNP and **echocardiography** assess injury, rhythm and function
★ **Cardiac MRI** identifies edema and nonischemic late gadolinium enhancement
Exclude ACS with coronary assessment when presentation/risk warrants; troponin alone cannot distinguish
Endomyocardial biopsy for selected fulminant, arrhythmic or unexplained progressive disease when etiology changes treatment
Routine broad viral serology rarely establishes myocardial cause

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Stable systolic HF → **diuresis and guideline-directed HF drugs**; defer beta blocker during shock
Hemodynamic compromise → ICU, vasopressors/inotropes and temporary mechanical circulatory support when refractory
Treat arrhythmias/AV block; pacing or defibrillation support when necessary
No routine steroids for presumed viral disease; giant-cell, eosinophilic and immune-mediated forms may need immunosuppression
Avoid NSAIDs for isolated myocarditis with HF; pericarditic pain requires individualized assessment

rows.label: Complications
items: Dilated cardiomyopathy, persistent HF, ventricular tachycardia, sudden death and intracardiac thrombosis

rows.label: Prevention
items: ★ Restrict strenuous exercise during active inflammation; return after symptom, imaging and rhythm reassessment
Classic restriction 3–6 months; newer guidance allows earlier individualized return in selected fully recovered athletes
Follow-up echo/MRI, ambulatory ECG and exercise testing guide clearance

rows.label: Mimics
items: MI: coronary distribution ischemia/scar and culprit artery
Stress cardiomyopathy: characteristic reversible wall-motion pattern
Pericarditis alone: pericardial inflammation without myocardial dysfunction

neonatal-intestinal-obstruction.name: Neonatal intestinal obstruction
neonatal-intestinal-obstruction.scope: Malrotation with midgut volvulus, duodenal atresia, jejunoileal atresia, meconium ileus, Hirschsprung disease, bilious vomiting, upper GI contrast series, Ladd procedure
neonatal-intestinal-obstruction.core: Bilious vomiting in a neonate is intestinal obstruction until proved otherwise; volvulus must be excluded before bowel ischemia develops.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Polyhydramnios → prenatal proximal obstruction; Down syndrome → duodenal atresia
CF → meconium ileus; trisomy 21 → Hirschsprung disease
Prematurity increases alternative risk of necrotizing enterocolitis

rows.label: Clues
items: Proximal obstruction → early vomiting with little distention; distal obstruction → marked distention
No meconium by **48 hours**, explosive stool after rectal exam → distal aganglionosis
★ Bloody stool, tenderness, shock or metabolic acidosis → ischemic bowel; urgent surgery

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Malrotation leaves narrow mesenteric base → twisting of bowel and mesenteric blood supply
Duodenal atresia: failed recanalization; jejunoileal atresia: fetal vascular injury
Hirschsprung: absent enteric ganglia → failure of distal relaxation and proximal dilation

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **Abdominal radiograph** first; double bubble without distal gas supports duodenal atresia
★ Suspected malrotation, stable → **upper GI contrast series**; corkscrew/abnormal duodenojejunal junction
Distal obstruction → contrast enema to characterize microcolon, meconium or transition zone
Hirschsprung confirmation → **rectal suction biopsy**, absent ganglion cells
Peritonitis or unstable suspected volvulus → exploration without delaying for contrast

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ All suspected obstruction → **NPO, orogastric decompression, IV fluids**, pediatric surgery
Volvulus → emergency Ladd procedure, detorsion and viability assessment; broad antibiotics if ischemic
Atresias → operative repair after stabilization; duodenal repair commonly duodenoduodenostomy
Uncomplicated meconium ileus → water-soluble contrast enema with hydration; complicated cases → surgery
Hirschsprung → irrigations then pull-through; enterocolitis → fluids, decompression, IV broad antibiotics

rows.label: Complications
items: Bowel necrosis, perforation, sepsis, short-bowel syndrome; Hirschsprung-associated enterocolitis can be fatal
Delayed diagnosis causes aspiration, electrolyte depletion and growth failure

rows.label: Mimics
items: Pyloric stenosis: nonbilious projectile emesis at several weeks
NEC: ill preterm infant, pneumatosis intestinalis
Physiologic reflux: thriving infant without bile or distention

table.title: Distal obstruction clues
rows: Narrow distal segment, proximal transition zone

neonatal-intestinal-obstruction.evidence: Not checked online; established neonatal surgical teaching.

nephrotic-syndrome.name: Nephrotic syndrome
nephrotic-syndrome.scope: Minimal change, FSGS, membranous, diabetic nephropathy; thrombosis and hyperlipidemia
nephrotic-syndrome.core: Heavy proteinuria with hypoalbuminemia and edema indicates nephrotic syndrome; assess the cause and complications before choosing immunosuppression.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Diabetes, obesity, HIV, hepatitis B/C, autoimmune disease, malignancy and selected medications
Children favor minimal change; obesity, HIV or reduced nephron mass can cause secondary FSGS

rows.label: Clues
items: Periorbital/dependent edema, foamy urine, weight gain; severe cases → anasarca or effusions
Hyperlipidemia, lipiduria, oval fat bodies/fatty casts; urine sediment often otherwise bland
★ Sudden flank pain, hematuria or falling filtration → **renal vein thrombosis**
Low effective volume may coexist with generalized fluid overload

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Podocyte barrier damage leaks albumin; sodium retention and low oncotic pressure promote edema
Urinary loss of anticoagulants and immunoglobulins increases thrombosis and infection risk

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ Adult protein **>3.5 g/day** or equivalent spot protein/creatinine ratio; serum albumin and lipid profile
Urinalysis/microscopy, renal function, HbA1c; targeted HIV, HBV/HCV, ANA/complement and monoclonal-protein studies
★ Most unexplained adult cases → **kidney biopsy**; classic childhood minimal change often treated empirically
Anti-PLA2R supports primary membranous disease; assess secondary causes and age-based cancer screening
Diabetes with retinopathy, gradually rising albuminuria → likely diabetic nephropathy; atypical features → consider biopsy

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Salt restriction, **loop diuretic**, ACE inhibitor/ARB for proteinuria; monitor perfusion and K
Eligible CKD → SGLT2 inhibitor; treat diabetes/infection or remove causative drug
Minimal change/primary FSGS → glucocorticoids; secondary FSGS → cause-directed/supportive treatment, not routine steroids
Membranous disease → risk-stratified observation versus rituximab or other immunosuppression
★ Confirmed thrombosis → anticoagulate; preventive anticoagulation individualized by albumin, pathology and bleeding risk

rows.label: Complications
items: DVT/PE, renal vein thrombosis, cellulitis/peritonitis, AKI, accelerated atherosclerosis
Progressive glomerular scarring can lead to kidney failure

rows.label: Prevention
items: Vaccinate, control BP/glycemia, avoid NSAIDs; monitor treatment toxicity and recurrent proteinuria

rows.label: Mimics
items: Nephritic syndrome: dysmorphic RBCs/casts, hypertension, inflammatory sediment
Cirrhosis: low albumin without nephrotic protein loss

table.title: Classic pathology
rows: Diffuse foot-process effacement; normal light microscopy

nephrotic-syndrome.evidence: Not checked online; established nephrology teaching and risk-based treatment principles.

neurocutaneous-disorders.name: Neurocutaneous disorders
neurocutaneous-disorders.scope: Neurofibromatosis type 1, neurofibromatosis type 2, tuberous sclerosis, Sturge-Weber syndrome, von Hippel-Lindau disease, ataxia-telangiectasia
neurocutaneous-disorders.core: Characteristic skin or ocular lesions plus neurologic tumors, seizures, or progressive ataxia suggest an inherited or mosaic multisystem disorder.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: NF1, NF2-related schwannomatosis, TSC, VHL: autosomal dominant; frequent de novo variants
Ataxia-telangiectasia: autosomal recessive; Sturge-Weber: sporadic somatic mosaicism

rows.label: Clues
items: ★ **Changing painful neurofibroma**, rapid growth, or new weakness → malignant transformation concern
Early focal seizures or developmental regression → evaluate structural cerebral lesions
NF2: hearing loss/tinnitus; NF1: cutaneous neurofibromas and childhood learning difficulties

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Tumor suppressor dysfunction → hamartomas or neoplasms; ATM defect → impaired DNA repair

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **Clinical pattern + genetic testing**; targeted MRI for neurologic or tumor symptoms
NF1: ≥2 criteria; ≥6 café-au-lait macules, size >5 mm prepubertal, >15 mm postpubertal
TSC: two major features or one major plus two minor; pathogenic variant also diagnostic

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Symptomatic tumors → specialist resection; TSC growing lesions → **everolimus** in selected cases
TSC infantile spasms → vigabatrin; other seizures → antiseizure drugs
Sturge-Weber seizures → levetiracetam; refractory focal epilepsy → surgical evaluation
Ataxia-telangiectasia: rehabilitation, infection treatment; minimize ionizing radiation

rows.label: Complications
items: NF1: malignant peripheral nerve sheath tumor; VHL: renal carcinoma and pheochromocytoma
TSC: hydrocephalus, renal hemorrhage; ataxia-telangiectasia: lymphoma/leukemia, recurrent sinopulmonary infections

rows.label: Prevention
items: ★ **Genetic counseling**; syndrome-specific eye, hearing, renal, and tumor surveillance
Sturge-Weber: ophthalmology follow-up for glaucoma; NF1: childhood BP and vision monitoring

rows.label: Mimics
items: Isolated café-au-lait macules: no additional diagnostic criteria
Friedreich ataxia: areflexia, cardiomyopathy, no ocular telangiectasias

table.title: Signature findings
rows: Axillary freckling, Lisch nodules, optic glioma
Ash-leaf macules, angiofibromas, cortical tubers, renal angiomyolipomas

neurocutaneous-disorders.evidence: Not checked online; established clinical genetics teaching.

normal-pediatric-variants.name: Normal pediatric variants
normal-pediatric-variants.scope: Thymic sail sign on chest radiograph, physiologic genu varum and valgum, tibial torsion, infantile hemangioma
normal-pediatric-variants.core: Age-appropriate anatomy and growth can resemble disease; symmetry, normal function, and expected evolution support reassurance instead of unnecessary intervention.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Normal skeletal alignment changes with development; familial rotational profiles are common
Infantile hemangiomas more frequent with prematurity, low birth weight and female sex

rows.label: Clues
items: ★ **Symmetric painless findings with normal growth/function** favor physiologic variation
Asymmetry, pain, progression, short stature or abnormal neurologic examination → pathologic evaluation
Hemangiomas appear in first weeks, proliferate rapidly during infancy, then gradually involute
Periocular, airway/beard-distribution, ulcerating or large segmental lesions are high-risk, not simple cosmetic variants

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Growth remodels lower-limb alignment/rotation; normal thymic tissue may silhouette against the lung
Hemangioma is a benign vascular tumor with proliferative and involution phases, distinct from vascular malformation

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ Typical symmetric limb variant → **clinical examination**, growth review and rotational profile
Imaging for red flags, atypical age or suspected metabolic bone disease; not routine physiologic bowing
Typical hemangioma → clinical diagnosis; ≥5 cutaneous lesions → hepatic ultrasound
Large segmental facial/lumbosacral lesion → evaluate associated structural anomalies with specialist guidance

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ **Reassurance and observation** for physiologic alignment and typical thymic appearance
Special shoes/braces do not correct internal tibial torsion; persistent severe functional deformity → orthopedics
★ High-risk hemangioma → **early referral, oral propranolol**; selected superficial lesions → topical timolol
Give propranolol with feeds, hold during poor intake/vomiting; monitor bradycardia and hypoglycemia

rows.label: Complications
items: Unnecessary imaging, bracing or surgery; hemangioma → ulceration, amblyopia, airway obstruction or residual skin change
Multiple hepatic hemangiomas → high-output heart failure or consumptive hypothyroidism

rows.label: Mimics
items: Blount disease: progressive asymmetric tibial bowing; rickets: widened wrists, abnormal mineralization
Mediastinal mass: mass effect/distortion rather than soft thymic contour

normal-pediatric-variants.evidence: Hemangioma guidance checked 2026-10-30: [AAP 2019 guideline](https://publications.aap.org/pediatrics/article/143/1/e20183475/37268/Clinical-Practice-Guideline-for-the-Management-of); skeletal variants: established teaching.

pediatric-abdominal-masses.name: Pediatric abdominal masses
pediatric-abdominal-masses.scope: Wilms tumor (nephroblastoma, WAGR, Beckwith-Wiedemann), neuroblastoma (adrenal medulla, crosses midline, catecholamines, N-myc), hydronephrosis, hepatoblastoma, ultrasound evaluation
pediatric-abdominal-masses.core: A child's abdominal mass: establish its organ of origin before biopsy; renal, sympathetic, hepatic, and obstructive lesions require different management.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: ★ Wilms: **WAGR**—aniridia, genitourinary anomalies, intellectual disability
Wilms: Beckwith-Wiedemann—macroglossia, omphalocele, hemihyperplasia
Hepatoblastoma: very low birth weight, Beckwith-Wiedemann, familial adenomatous polyposis
Hydronephrosis: congenital urinary obstruction or vesicoureteral reflux

rows.label: Clues
items: Often found incidentally during bathing; persistent enlargement, weight loss, pallor suggest malignancy
Neuroblastoma dissemination: periorbital ecchymoses, bone pain; opsoclonus-myoclonus possible
★ Weakness, gait change, bladder dysfunction → possible spinal cord compression

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Wilms: embryonal renal tumor; neuroblastoma: neural crest-derived adrenal medulla or sympathetic chain
Hepatoblastoma: embryonal hepatic malignancy; hydronephrosis: collecting-system dilation

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **Abdominal ultrasound** first → solid versus cystic and renal versus extrarenal origin
Solid lesion → contrast CT/MRI abdomen; chest imaging for malignant staging
Neuroblastoma: tissue diagnosis, MYCN testing, MIBG imaging, bone marrow assessment for staging
MYCN amplification → unfavorable prognosis; age and stage also determine neuroblastoma risk

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Suspected Wilms: avoid repeated vigorous palpation and routine percutaneous biopsy; US approach usually nephrectomy first
Wilms: surgery + vincristine/dactinomycin-based chemotherapy; radiation for higher-risk disease
Neuroblastoma: low risk → observation/resection; high risk → chemotherapy, surgery, transplant, anti-GD2 immunotherapy
Hepatoblastoma: cisplatin-based chemotherapy + resection; unresectable liver-confined disease → transplant evaluation
Hydronephrosis: infected obstruction → urgent drainage; progressive functional loss → corrective surgery

rows.label: Complications
items: Tumor rupture/spillage worsens Wilms staging; bilateral disease threatens renal function
Hydronephrosis → infection, renal injury; neuroblastoma → marrow failure or cord compression

rows.label: Prevention
items: Syndrome-specific abdominal ultrasound surveillance for children predisposed to embryonal tumors

rows.label: Mimics
items: Constipation: fecal loading, improves after stool evacuation
Ovarian mass: pelvic/adnexal origin; torsion causes acute pain

pediatric-exanthems.name: Pediatric exanthems
pediatric-exanthems.scope: Measles (rubeola), rubella (German measles), roseola infantum (HHV-6), erythema infectiosum (parvovirus B19 fifth disease), scarlet fever, varicella, clinical appearance, complications
pediatric-exanthems.core: Fever with a childhood rash: use fever timing, rash progression, mucosal findings, immunization status, and pregnancy exposure to distinguish causes.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Incomplete immunization, daycare/school exposure, travel; immunosuppression increases severe viral disease
Pregnant contacts require prompt assessment after rubella, parvovirus, or varicella exposure

rows.label: Clues
items: ★ **Toxic appearance**, petechiae/purpura, hypotension, meningismus → evaluate invasive infection immediately
Measles: cough, coryza, conjunctivitis precede rash; rubella: posterior auricular/suboccipital adenopathy
Varicella: trunk/scalp predominance; oral mucosal lesions may accompany the skin eruption

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Parvovirus suppresses erythroid precursors; congenital infection can cause severe fetal anemia
VZV remains latent in sensory ganglia; HHV-6 commonly causes febrile illness in infants

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ Suspected measles → **airborne isolation**, notify public health; respiratory PCR plus serum IgM
Scarlet fever → rapid GAS test; negative pediatric test → throat culture
Typical roseola/fifth disease: clinical; atypical vesicles → VZV PCR; rubella → public-health serology/PCR

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Scarlet fever → **penicillin or amoxicillin**; other uncomplicated exanthems generally supportive
Measles → hydration, complication care, clinician-supervised vitamin A for children
Severe/immunocompromised varicella → **IV acyclovir**; avoid aspirin in children

rows.label: Complications
items: Measles: pneumonia, encephalitis, delayed SSPE; rubella: congenital cataracts, deafness, PDA
Parvovirus: aplastic crisis, hydrops; roseola: febrile seizures
Varicella: bacterial superinfection, pneumonia, cerebellitis; GAS: rheumatic fever, glomerulonephritis

rows.label: Prevention
items: ★ **MMR and varicella vaccines**; live vaccines contraindicated during pregnancy and severe immunosuppression
Measles exposure: MMR within 72 hours or immune globulin within 6 days for eligible contacts

rows.label: Mimics
items: Kawasaki disease: ≥5 days fever, conjunctivitis, oral/extremity changes
Drug eruption: medication exposure without characteristic infectious sequence

table.title: Signature rash
rows: Koplik spots; face → downward confluent rash
Sandpaper rash, Pastia lines, strawberry tongue

pediatric-hip-disorders.name: Pediatric hip disorders
pediatric-hip-disorders.scope: Developmental dysplasia of the hip, Legg-Calve-Perthes disease, slipped capital femoral epiphysis, transient synovitis, pediatric limp workup
pediatric-hip-disorders.core: A child’s limp or knee pain may originate in the hip; age, weight-bearing ability, and hip rotation separate common developmental disorders.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Breech presentation, female sex, family history → developmental hip dysplasia
Obesity and adolescence → slipped capital femoral epiphysis; atypically young/thin cases suggest endocrine disease
Recent viral illness → transient synovitis; Perthes often boys aged 4–8 years

rows.label: Clues
items: Infant asymmetric abduction or leg length; older child limp, groin/thigh/knee pain
★ **Fever, toxic appearance, refusal to bear weight**, painful restricted motion → septic arthritis concern
SCFE: obligate external rotation with flexion; Perthes: gradual painless/painful limp with limited internal rotation

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Dysplasia: shallow acetabulum and unstable femoral head; Perthes: femoral-head avascular necrosis
SCFE: physeal failure displaces epiphysis relative to neck; synovitis: transient sterile joint inflammation

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **Examine hip in unexplained knee pain**; assess gait, rotation, fever, neurologic signs
DDH: Ortolani reduces dislocation; Barlow provokes instability; limited abduction more useful after early infancy
Risk-based DDH imaging → ultrasound around 6 weeks; radiograph after femoral ossification, usually ≥4–6 months
Suspected septic hip → CBC, ESR/CRP, cultures, ultrasound for effusion → urgent aspiration
Kocher features: fever >38.5°C, nonweight-bearing, WBC >12,000, ESR >40; support concern, never replace aspiration

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Suspected SCFE → **immediate nonweight-bearing**, orthopedic fixation; no forceful manipulation
★ Septic joint → **urgent drainage + IV antibiotics** after cultures when feasible
Transient synovitis → rest, NSAID, close reassessment; persistent/worsening symptoms require renewed evaluation
Perthes → orthopedic containment/ROM plan; DDH treatment depends on age and stability below

rows.label: Complications
items: Untreated dysplasia → early osteoarthritis; SCFE → avascular necrosis/chondrolysis
Perthes → femoral-head deformity; missed septic arthritis → irreversible joint destruction

rows.label: Prevention
items: Newborn and infant hip examinations; avoid tight swaddling with extended adducted hips

rows.label: Mimics
items: Osteomyelitis: focal bony tenderness, MRI marrow changes
Trauma: injury history and fracture imaging

pediatric-hip-disorders.evidence: Not checked online; established pediatric orthopedic assessment principles.

pertussis.name: Pertussis
pertussis.scope: Bordetella pertussis, catarrhal, paroxysmal, and convalescent stages, posttussive emesis, inspiratory whoop, macrolide therapy, postexposure prophylaxis, Tdap vaccination
pertussis.core: Prolonged paroxysmal cough with posttussive emesis; infants may present with apnea and cyanosis without a whoop.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Unvaccinated/undervaccinated children, waning immunity in adolescents/adults, infected household contacts
Young infants have greatest risk of severe disease; vaccinated individuals can still transmit infection

rows.label: Clues
items: Catarrhal stage: rhinorrhea, mild cough, little or no fever; greatest early infectiousness
Inspiratory whoop often absent in adolescents/adults; convalescence can last weeks with recurrent cough
★ Infant **marked lymphocytosis**, poor feeding, or respiratory compromise; minimal fever despite serious illness

rows.label: Pathophys
items: B. pertussis adheres to respiratory cilia; toxin-mediated injury impairs mucus clearance
Pertussis toxin inhibits Gi signaling; impaired lymphocyte extravasation causes circulating lymphocytosis

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **Nasopharyngeal PCR** during first 3–4 weeks of cough; posterior nasopharynx, not throat swab
Culture most useful in first 2 weeks; late illness → validated serology when available
Treat suspected high-risk cases before results; chest imaging for respiratory compromise or suspected pneumonia

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ **Azithromycin** preferred; TMP-SMX alternative at age ≥2 months when macrolides unsuitable
Best symptom benefit early; later treatment mainly reduces transmission within infectious window
Treat age ≥1 year within 3 weeks of cough; infants/pregnancy up to 6 weeks
Hospitalize young infants or apnea/hypoxemia; oxygen, suction, hydration and cardiorespiratory monitoring
Infant macrolides carry pyloric stenosis risk, but benefit outweighs risk; monitor vomiting

rows.label: Complications
items: Pneumonia, seizures/encephalopathy, infant pulmonary hypertension and death
Adults: rib fractures, syncope, stress incontinence from forceful coughing

rows.label: Prevention
items: ★ Droplet isolation until **5 days of effective antibiotics**, or 21 days from cough onset untreated
Household contacts → azithromycin prophylaxis within 21 days of index cough; also target high-risk exposures
DTaP childhood series; Tdap adolescent booster and once for adults without prior Tdap
★ **Tdap each pregnancy at 27–36 weeks**, preferably early in that interval

rows.label: Mimics
items: Viral bronchitis: improving ordinary cough without characteristic paroxysms or epidemiologic link
Asthma: recurrent wheeze/trigger pattern, reversible airflow obstruction
Chlamydial infant pneumonia: afebrile staccato cough, eosinophilia, often prior conjunctivitis

physician-patient-communication.name: Physician-patient communication
physician-patient-communication.scope: Medical interpreters, limited English proficiency, delivering bad news, empathetic communication, family requests to withhold information
physician-patient-communication.core: Respect autonomy through understandable, honest, empathic dialogue; identify what patients understand and want before sharing decisions or sensitive information.

rows.label: Principle
items: Confidentiality, cultural humility, informed choice; language barriers never imply impaired capacity
Patient preferences determine family involvement and desired level of disclosure

rows.label: Do
items: ★ **Qualified medical interpreter**, free to patient; speak directly to patient in short segments
★ Bad news: privacy → understanding/preferences → warning → plain disclosure → empathy → plan
Validate emotion; open questions, silence, teach-back; explore beliefs before correcting misinformation

rows.label: Don't
items: Avoid jargon, false reassurance, interrupting, arguing, blaming, or premature advice
Avoid routine reliance on children/family for interpreting consent or sensitive discussions
Avoid promising cure or confidentiality beyond legal limits

rows.label: Exceptions
items: ★ **Family requests nondisclosure → ask patient privately**; patient preferences control disclosure
Capable patient may decline details or designate another recipient; document preference
Emergency without interpreter → temporary available help while securing qualified interpretation

rows.label: Traps
items: ★ **Therapeutic privilege is narrow**; anticipated distress alone never justifies withholding diagnosis
Anger → acknowledge concern, clarify cause, establish boundaries if threatening; no reflex discharge
Requested adult-family interpreter → verify suitability/privacy/voluntariness; offer professional

physician-patient-communication.evidence: Checked 2026-10-30: [HHS interpreter guidance](https://www.hhs.gov/civil-rights/for-individuals/faqs/may-an-lep-person-use-a-family-member-as-an-interpreter/index.html); established autonomy and bad-news communication principles.

pleural-effusion.name: Pleural effusion
pleural-effusion.scope: Transudate vs exudate (Light criteria), parapneumonic effusion, empyema, malignant effusion
pleural-effusion.core: Fluid in the pleural space causes dyspnea, dullness, and reduced breath sounds; classify by mechanism and identify infection requiring drainage.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Heart failure, cirrhosis, nephrotic syndrome; pneumonia, malignancy, pulmonary embolism, TB
Recent thoracic surgery, pancreatitis, esophageal rupture, autoimmune disease

rows.label: Clues
items: Pleuritic pain, reduced tactile fremitus; large effusion may shift mediastinum away
Fever or persistent sepsis despite antibiotics suggests complicated parapneumonic fluid
Bloody fluid suggests malignancy, embolism, or trauma; milky fluid suggests chyle

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Transudate: altered hydrostatic/oncotic pressure; exudate: increased permeability or impaired lymphatic drainage

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ Chest radiograph → **ultrasound-guided thoracentesis** for new unexplained, unilateral, or atypical effusion
Classic bilateral heart-failure effusions → diuresis first; sample if fever, asymmetry, or treatment failure
★ **Exudate if any Light criterion** positive; compare paired pleural and serum measurements
Pleural pH, glucose, cell differential, Gram stain/culture; cytology if cancer suspected
Diuresis can create pseudoexudate; serum–pleural albumin gradient >1.2 g/dL supports transudate

rows.label: Tx
items: Treat systemic cause; therapeutic thoracentesis for significant symptoms; avoid rapid excessive drainage
★ Pus, positive culture, or **pH ≤7.20** → chest tube plus antibiotics
Loculated infected fluid → intrapleural tPA/DNase; persistent sepsis → VATS evaluation
★ Recurrent symptomatic malignancy → **indwelling pleural catheter** or pleurodesis; trapped lung favors catheter

rows.label: Complications
items: Empyema, loculation, trapped lung, respiratory compromise
Thoracentesis → pneumothorax, bleeding, reexpansion pulmonary edema

rows.label: Prevention
items: Heart-failure control, prompt pneumonia treatment; ultrasound guidance reduces procedural injury

rows.label: Mimics
items: Atelectasis: mediastinal shift toward volume loss
Consolidation: increased fremitus, bronchial breath sounds
Pneumothorax: hyperresonance rather than dullness

pleural-effusion.evidence: Not checked online; established pleural disease teaching.

primary-immunodeficiencies.name: Primary immunodeficiencies
primary-immunodeficiencies.scope: Selective IgA deficiency, common variable immunodeficiency (CVID), X-linked agammaglobulinemia, severe combined immunodeficiency, hyper-IgE syndrome, Wiskott-Aldrich, chronic granulomatous disease
primary-immunodeficiencies.core: Recurrent, unusually severe, persistent, or opportunistic infections; organism pattern and age of onset localize the immune defect.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Consanguinity, affected relatives, male relatives dying in infancy; absent family history does not exclude disease

rows.label: Clues
items: ★ Failure to thrive, chronic diarrhea, persistent thrush, or infections across multiple organ systems
Deep abscesses suggest phagocyte dysfunction; recurrent encapsulated bacteria suggest impaired antibody function

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Selective IgA deficiency: impaired mucosal defense; respiratory infections, giardiasis, atopy, or no symptoms
Antibody disorders impair opsonization; T-cell defects permit viral, fungal, and protozoal opportunists

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ Start **CBC with differential, quantitative immunoglobulins**, HIV testing; assess vaccine antibody responses
Lymphocyte subsets distinguish B-cell and T-cell deficiencies; abnormal results → genetic confirmation
IgA deficiency: isolated IgA <7 mg/dL after age 4 years; normal IgG and IgM
★ Newborn **TREC screen** detects impaired T-cell production before symptomatic SCID

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Profound combined immune failure → isolation, irradiated CMV-negative blood products, urgent **transplant evaluation**
Acute infections: organism-directed antimicrobials; immunoglobulin replacement not useful for isolated IgA deficiency

rows.label: Complications
items: Bronchiectasis, chronic enteropathy, autoimmune disease; CVID additionally increases lymphoma risk
Anti-IgA antibodies can cause anaphylaxis to blood products

rows.label: Prevention
items: ★ Avoid **live vaccines** in major T-cell defects; immunize household contacts with safe vaccine choices
IgA-related transfusion reactions → washed cellular products or IgA-deficient plasma
CGD: TMP-SMX + itraconazole prophylaxis; genetic counseling for inherited defects

rows.label: Mimics
items: HIV: acquired CD4 depletion with positive virologic testing
Secondary hypogammaglobulinemia: nephrotic protein loss, B-cell malignancy, or rituximab exposure

table.title: Defect fingerprints
rows: Adolescent/adult; low IgG, poor vaccine response
Boy after 6 months; absent tonsils/B cells
Infant; absent thymic shadow, profound lymphopenia
Cold abscesses, eczema, retained teeth, pneumatoceles

primary-immunodeficiencies.evidence: Not checked online; established clinical immunology teaching.

pubertal-development.name: Pubertal development
pubertal-development.scope: Tanner stages, normal thelarche vs breast mass, premature adrenarche, precocious puberty, constitutional delay of growth and puberty
pubertal-development.core: Interpret sexual maturation by sequence, age, growth velocity, and bone age; isolated benign variants lack progressive gonadal activation.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Constitutional delay often familial; chronic illness, undernutrition, excess exercise delay maturation
CNS lesions, gonadal/adrenal hormone excess, exogenous sex steroids can cause early puberty

rows.label: Clues
items: Girls: breast budding precedes peak growth, then menarche about 2–3 years later
Boys: testes enlarge before penile growth; pubic hair reflects adrenarche, not necessarily gonadarche
★ Asymmetric tender **subareolar breast bud** at expected age usually normal; hard eccentric mass needs evaluation
Rapid height acceleration, advancing secondary characteristics, neurologic symptoms → pathologic early maturation concern

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Central puberty: hypothalamic GnRH pulsatility → LH/FSH → gonadal steroids
Adrenarche produces adrenal androgens independently; peripheral hormone excess suppresses pituitary gonadotropins

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ Precocious: secondary sexual development **before 8 years girls or 9 years boys**
★ Delayed: **no breasts by 13**, no testes ≥4 mL by 14; evaluate absent menarche by 15
Growth chart, Tanner examination, bone age; LH/FSH, estradiol/testosterone, TSH selected by pattern
Central precocity → pubertal basal/stimulated LH; brain MRI especially boys, young girls, neurologic signs
Peripheral pattern → targeted adrenal/gonadal tests/imaging; isolated adrenarche requires exclusion of rapid virilization

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Progressive central precocity → **GnRH agonist**; treat CNS cause when present
Peripheral precocity → remove hormone source or treat tumor/adrenal disorder; GnRH agonist alone ineffective
Constitutional delay → reassurance, follow growth; distress → specialist-guided brief sex-steroid course
Benign premature thelarche/adrenarche → observe progression; no automatic hormonal treatment

rows.label: Complications
items: Early epiphyseal closure → reduced adult height; psychosocial distress
Missed hypogonadism → impaired bone accrual; untreated CNS/tumor cause may progress

rows.label: Prevention
items: Adequate nutrition, manage chronic disease, avoid household hormone exposure; serial growth surveillance

rows.label: Mimics
items: Primary gonadal failure: high LH/FSH, low sex steroids
Permanent central hypogonadism: absent progression rather than eventual familial catch-up

pubertal-development.evidence: Not checked online; established pediatric endocrine timing and Tanner staging.

septic-arthritis.name: Septic arthritis
septic-arthritis.scope: Nongonococcal, gonococcal, prosthetic joint infection, IV drug use, empiric coverage (vancomycin + cefepime), contiguous osteomyelitis
septic-arthritis.core: Acutely painful swollen joint with restricted passive motion → urgent aspiration and drainage; delayed treatment rapidly destroys cartilage.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Prosthesis, recent surgery/injection, rheumatoid arthritis, immunosuppression, diabetes, bacteremia
IV drug use → S aureus and gram-negative risk, including Pseudomonas
Young sexually active adults → disseminated gonorrhea; adjacent ulcers/osteomyelitis → contiguous spread

rows.label: Clues
items: Usually acute monoarthritis, often knee; fever may be absent, especially in older/immunocompromised adults
★ **Severe pain with both active and passive motion**; inability to bear weight
Gonococcal dissemination: migratory polyarthralgia, tenosynovitis, sparse pustules; may progress to purulent monoarthritis
Prosthetic infection: persistent pain, loosening, wound drainage or sinus tract, sometimes minimal systemic illness

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Hematogenous seeding or direct inoculation → neutrophilic enzymes damage articular cartilage
Implant biofilm limits antibiotic eradication without surgical source control

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **Arthrocentesis before antibiotics** when stable: cell count/differential, Gram stain, culture, crystals
Synovial WBC >50,000/µL, neutrophil predominance supports infection; lower counts or negative Gram stain never exclude
★ **Crystals do not exclude infection**; send cultures even when gout seems likely
Blood cultures; gonococcal NAAT from exposed mucosal sites; MRI for suspected contiguous osteomyelitis

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ After cultures → **IV vancomycin + cefepime** for severe disease, IV drug use, gram-negative risk
Stable low-risk adult: vancomycin ± ceftriaxone based on exposure; narrow to organism/susceptibility
Sepsis → immediate antibiotics without delaying for aspiration; large joints usually need arthroscopic washout
Persistent symptoms → repeat drainage, seek abscess/osteomyelitis; mobilize after infection controlled

rows.label: Complications
items: Irreversible joint destruction, avascular necrosis, osteomyelitis, bacteremia, sepsis
Prolonged antibiotics → renal injury, line complications, C difficile; prolonged immobility → stiffness

rows.label: Prevention
items: Sterile procedures, treat skin infections, injection-harm reduction
Gonorrhea: treat partners, screen other STIs, abstain until treatment completed and partners treated

rows.label: Mimics
items: Crystal arthritis: polarized crystals; infection still possible concurrently
Bursitis: localized periarticular swelling, passive joint motion relatively preserved
Reactive arthritis: sterile inflammatory arthritis after GI/GU infection

table.title: Special treatment branches
rows: Debridement, implant retention, prolonged pathogen-directed antibiotics

shock.name: Shock
shock.scope: Hypovolemic, cardiogenic, distributive (septic, anaphylactic, neurogenic), obstructive, fluid resuscitation, vasopressors
shock.core: Circulatory failure causing tissue hypoperfusion; normal blood pressure does not exclude early shock.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Hemorrhage, GI losses, MI, infection, allergen exposure, spinal injury, thromboembolism
Recent surgery, immunosuppression, indwelling devices increase occult infection risk

rows.label: Clues
items: Tachycardia, altered mentation, oliguria, cool mottled skin; distributive forms may initially feel warm
★ **Anaphylaxis**: rapid airway swelling, wheezing, hypotension; skin findings may be absent
Neurogenic: hypotension with **bradycardia**, warm skin after spinal cord injury

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Oxygen delivery falls below demand → anaerobic metabolism, lactate accumulation
Distributive vasodilation → relative hypovolemia despite normal total body fluid

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **Bedside ultrasound**: cardiac function, pericardial fluid, RV dilation, lung sliding, volume assessment
Serial lactate, capillary refill, urine output; CBC, chemistry, ECG, troponin; cultures if infection suspected
Septic shock: vasopressors for MAP ≥65 plus lactate >2 despite volume resuscitation

rows.label: Tx
items: Airway/oxygen, IV access; **balanced crystalloid**, dynamic fluid-response reassessment; restrict with pulmonary congestion
★ Hemorrhage → **control bleeding + balanced blood products**; avoid large crystalloid loads
★ Septic shock → antibiotics within 1 hour, drainage/debridement; crystalloid 30 mL/kg within 3 hours
★ Persistent septic hypotension → **norepinephrine**, MAP ≥65; add vasopressin, then epinephrine; refractory → hydrocortisone

rows.label: Complications
items: AKI, ischemic hepatitis, DIC, ARDS, bowel ischemia, multiorgan failure
Excess fluids → edema; vasopressors → digital/mesenteric ischemia

rows.label: Prevention
items: Early infection treatment, catheter hygiene, VTE prophylaxis, hemorrhage control
After anaphylaxis: trigger avoidance, epinephrine autoinjector, allergy referral

rows.label: Mimics
items: Vasovagal syncope: transient bradycardia, rapid recovery supine
Hypoglycemia: low bedside glucose, improvement with dextrose

table.title: Hemodynamics and cause-directed rescue
rows: Decompress pneumothorax; drain tamponade; reperfuse PE

thrombocytopenia.name: Thrombocytopenia
thrombocytopenia.scope: Evaluation of isolated thrombocytopenia, peripheral smear, immune thrombocytopenia, drug-induced, procedural platelet thresholds
thrombocytopenia.core: Low platelet count requires confirmation and distinction among impaired production, immune destruction, consumption, sequestration, and laboratory artifact.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Recent infection, autoimmune disease, HIV/HCV, lymphoproliferative disease → secondary immune thrombocytopenia
Heparin, quinine, TMP-SMX, vancomycin; alcohol, marrow-suppressive drugs; cirrhosis with splenic sequestration

rows.label: Clues
items: Petechiae, purpura, epistaxis, gingival bleeding; mucosal hemorrhage signals clinically important platelet disorder
★ **Neurologic/renal abnormalities + hemolysis** → thrombotic microangiopathy; systemic illness/coagulopathy → DIC
Heparin exposure + >50% platelet decline, thrombosis, typical 5–10-day onset → HIT

rows.label: Pathophys
items: ITP: IgG-mediated platelet clearance and impaired megakaryocyte production
Drug-dependent immune destruction often causes abrupt severe counts; HIT activates platelets, producing thrombosis

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **Repeat CBC + peripheral smear**; platelet clumps → citrate tube for pseudothrombocytopenia
Isolated low platelets, normal coagulation, large platelets → ITP after excluding secondary causes
Schistocytes → LDH, haptoglobin, creatinine, coagulation studies; suspected TTP → urgent ADAMTS13 sample
HIV/HCV testing for new ITP; marrow biopsy only atypical cytopenias or suspected marrow disease
4Ts estimates HIT probability; intermediate/high → PF4 immunoassay, functional confirmation

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Adult ITP **<30,000/µL or bleeding → glucocorticoid**; children without significant bleeding → observation
★ ITP critical bleeding → **IVIG + high-dose steroid + platelet transfusion**
Drug immune thrombocytopenia → stop culprit; persistent ITP → rituximab, thrombopoietin agonist, or selected splenectomy
Suspected TTP → plasma exchange; HIT → stop heparin, start argatroban/nonheparin anticoagulant
Older board LP target: 50,000/µL; current trigger below; neurosurgical targets often ≥100,000/µL

rows.label: Complications
items: Intracranial hemorrhage with severe disease; thrombosis in HIT/TTP
Steroid toxicity, immunosuppression; splenectomy → encapsulated bacterial sepsis

rows.label: Prevention
items: Avoid culprit rechallenge, aspirin/NSAIDs when bleeding risk high; vaccinate before splenectomy

rows.label: Mimics
items: Von Willebrand disease: often normal platelet count with mucocutaneous bleeding
Marrow failure: additional cytopenias, abnormal precursor morphology

thrombocytopenia.evidence: Checked 2026-10-30: [AABB/ICTMG platelet recommendations (2025)](https://www.aabb.org/news-resources/news/article/2025/05/29/aabb-develops-new-platelet-transfusion-guidelines); other hematology principles not separately checked.

urinary-tract-infections.name: Urinary tract infections
urinary-tract-infections.scope: Asymptomatic bacteriuria, acute cystitis, pyelonephritis, catheter-associated urinary tract infection (CAUTI), catheter removal, empiric antibiotics
urinary-tract-infections.core: Symptoms localize urinary infection: bladder disease lacks systemic illness; renal involvement causes fever or flank pain; bacteriuria alone is insufficient.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Sexual activity, spermicides, pregnancy, obstruction/stones, urinary retention, instrumentation
Catheter duration, diabetes, prior resistant isolates or antibiotics increase complicated-course risk

rows.label: Clues
items: Dysuria, frequency, urgency, suprapubic discomfort; absent vaginal discharge supports urinary source
★ **Rigors, CVA tenderness, vomiting, hypotension** → pyelonephritis or urosepsis
Catheterized patients: new urinary/systemic symptoms; cloudy urine or pyuria alone insufficient

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Usually ascending enteric bacteria, predominantly E coli; catheter biofilm maintains colonization
Urease-producing Proteus alkalinizes urine → struvite calculi and persistent infection

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **Urinalysis**: pyuria, leukocyte esterase, nitrites; negative nitrites do not exclude infection
Culture: pyelonephritis, pregnancy, CAUTI, recurrence/resistance; classic cystitis often clinical
Persistent fever after 48–72 hours, sepsis, or suspected obstruction → renal imaging
Asymptomatic bacteriuria: usually ≥100,000 CFU/mL; delirium alone → seek other causes without automatic antibiotics

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ **Treat asymptomatic bacteriuria only in pregnancy or before urologic mucosal trauma** in routine adult scenarios
★ CAUTI → **remove unnecessary catheter**; if needed and present >2 weeks, replace before culture/treatment
★ Infected obstructed collecting system → **urgent drainage + IV antibiotics**; antibiotics alone insufficient
Improving nonpregnant pyelonephritis: fluoroquinolone 5–7 days, other active drugs 7 days; high-risk cases individualized

Antibiotics → resistance, C difficile; fluoroquinolones → tendon injury, QT prolongation

Postmenopausal recurrence → vaginal estrogen; selected recurrences → postcoital/continuous antibiotic prophylaxis
